docs.title: 🌐 Computer Networks: Modern Course Knowledge Repository & Interactive Learning Guide
docs.text: An open-source, beautifully structured, visual, and mathematically rigorous educational repository for mastering Computer Networking from A to Z. Designed to feel like a modern interactive documentation platform and full-fledged university/industry curriculum.

docs.text:

docs.title: 📑 4. Standard Learning Template
docs.text:
Every chapter and topic guide in this repository strictly adheres to a uniform 12-section pedagogical blueprint (Standard 12-Section Template):

# Section Description & Scope 01 Overview Topic Introduction, Context, and Architectural Motivation 02 Learning Objectives Clear, actionable competency goals and key learning outcomes 03 Core Concepts In-depth rigorous theoretical mechanisms and formal definitions 04 Visual Explanation High-definition ASCII architectural schematics and Mermaid sequence flows 05 Step-by-Step Mechanism Algorithmic state-transition walkthroughs and step-by-step traces 06 Real-Life Example Concrete real-world analogies and operational production use-cases 07 Practical Implementation Python packet analysis scripts, simulation code, or calculation models 08 Common Mistakes Frequently tested pitfalls, subtle edge cases, and conceptual traps 09 Practice Problems Authentic university final/midterm exam problems with rigorous step-by-step solutions 10 Knowledge Check Conceptual multiple-choice questions with comprehensive diagnostic answer keys 11 Summary & Revision Sheet Quick-reference revision summary tables and key mental models 12 References Official IETF RFC citations, authoritative textbook chapters, and documentation

docs.title: 📁 Module 01: Network Basics and Architecture
docs.text:
• 01-internet-and-network-core.md: Network Edge, Core mesh, Circuit Switching (FDM vs TDM, slot calculation) vs Packet Switching (Statistical Multiplexing, Binomial probability).
  • 02-delay-loss-and-throughput.md: The 4 Nodal Delays (\(d_{proc}, d_{que}, d_{trans}, d_{prop}\)), Caravan Analogy, Multi-hop delay calculations, Bottleneck Link Throughput.
  • 03-layering-and-encapsulation.md: OSI 7-Layer vs TCP/IP 5-Layer model, Postal Analogy, Hop-by-hop traversal across Hubs (L1), Switches (L2), and Routers (L3), Protocol Headers & Addressing changes.

docs.title: 📁 Module 02: Network Security Fundamentals
docs.text:
• 01-cia-triad-and-cryptography.md: CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability), Symmetric/Asymmetric Ciphers, Digital Signatures, Hash functions.
  • 02-network-attacks-and-defense.md: Packet Sniffing (Wireshark/Promiscuous mode), IP Spoofing, Denial of Service (DoS) & Distributed DoS (Botnets/SYN flood), Firewalls & Packet Filters.

docs.title: 📁 Module 03: Application Layer and Protocols
docs.text:
• 01-application-architectures.md: Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer (P2P), Sockets as application doors, Port numbers vs IP addresses.
  • 02-http-and-web-caching.md: HTTP 1.0 vs 1.1, Non-Persistent vs Persistent HTTP Timing (\(2\text{RTT} + \text{FTT}\) vs \(\text{RTT} + n(\text{RTT} + \text{FTT})\)), Web Caching & Proxy Servers, Cookies.
  • 03-email-protocols-smtp.md: Email architecture (User Agents, Mail Transfer Agents, Mailboxes, Outgoing Queues), SMTP (Push, Port 25) vs HTTP/POP3/IMAP (Pull).
  • 04-dns-domain-name-system.md: Hierarchical DNS Architecture (Root, TLD, Authoritative, Local DNS), Iterative vs Recursive Queries, Resource Records (A, NS, CNAME, MX), Local Caching.

docs.title: 📁 Module 04: Transport Layer and Reliability
docs.text:
• 01-transport-multiplexing.md: Port-based Multiplexing (MUX at sender) and Demultiplexing (DEMUX at receiver), Connectionless vs Connection-Oriented demux.
  • 02-udp-and-internet-checksum.md: UDP Datagram format, 16-bit Internet Checksum calculation with 1's complement wrap-around addition in Binary and Hexadecimal.
  • 03-reliable-data-transfer.md: RDT 1.0 through 3.0, Stop-and-Wait (No Loss, Data Loss, ACK Loss, Delayed ACK), Pipelining principles, Go-Back-N (GBN) vs Selective Repeat (SR).
  • 04-tcp-principles-and-handshake.md: TCP Segment anatomy, Sequence numbers (starting byte) and ACK numbers (next expected byte), 3-Way Handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), 4-Way Connection Close (FIN, ACK).
  • 05-tcp-flow-and-congestion-control.md: Flow Control (Receiver Window \(rwnd\)), Congestion Control principles, Slow Start (exponential growth), AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease sawtooth), Triple Duplicate ACKs vs Timeout recovery.

docs.title: 📁 Module 05: Network Layer and Routing
docs.text:
• 01-network-layer-overview.md: Data Plane vs Control Plane, Forwarding (local per-router action) vs Routing (network-wide path computation).
  • 02-ipv4-and-fragmentation.md: IPv4 Header structure, MTU limitations, 8-Byte Boundary division rule, More Fragment Flag (\(M\)), Fragmentation offset calculation tables.
  • 03-dhcp-dynamic-addressing.md: Plug-and-Play dynamic IP configuration, The 4-step DORA exchange (Discover, Offer, Request, ACK) over UDP ports 67 and 68.
  • 04-nat-network-address-translation.md: Private IPv4 addressing (RFC 1918), NAT Translation Table mechanics, 4-step packet header transformation (LAN Private IP:Port \(\leftrightarrow\) WAN Public IP:NAT Port).
  • 05-routing-algorithms-dijkstra.md: Link State Routing, Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm step-by-step iteration table, Least Cost Path Tree construction, Router Forwarding Table generation.

docs.title: 📁 Module 06: Data Link Layer and Local Area Networks
docs.text:
• 01-link-layer-and-error-detection.md: Link layer services, Framing, Parity checks, Two-dimensional parity, Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) Polynomial Division.
  • 02-multiple-access-protocols.md: Broadcast channels, Channel Partitioning (TDMA, FDMA, CDMA), Random Access (Slotted ALOHA, Pure ALOHA, CSMA/CD collision detection), Taking-Turns (Polling, Token Ring).
  • 03-mac-addressing-and-arp.md: 48-bit MAC Addresses, Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), Broadcast Query (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) and Unicast Reply, Cross-Subnet packet delivery through Default Gateway Routers.

docs.title: 📁 Module 07: Master Cheat Sheets and Formulas
docs.text: • master-formula-cheat-sheet.md: Every mathematical formula in Computer Networks consolidated into a single ultra-fast revision guide (Delays, Throughput, TDM/FDM, HTTP RTT, TCP Checksum, Fragmentation, Subnetting, Dijkstra, CRC).

docs.title: 📦 Module 01: Network Basics & Architecture
docs.text: Welcome to Module 01: Network Basics & Architecture. This foundational module establishes how the global Internet is physically structured, how data travels across the network core via circuit and packet switching, how delays and bottlenecks occur, and how layered architectures (OSI & TCP/IP) enable multi-vendor interoperability through encapsulation.

docs.title: 🎯 Key Competencies Acquired
docs.text: By completing this module, you will be able to: 1. Differentiate precisely between dedicated circuit switching and shared packet switching. 2. Calculate transmission time over TDM slots and evaluate packet switching user capacity using Binomial distributions. 3. Compute exact nodal and end-to-end delays across complex multi-router paths (\(d_{nodal} = d_{proc} + d_{que} + d_{trans} + d_{prop}\)). 4. Identify bottleneck links in networks and compute end-to-end effective throughput. 5. Trace a data payload as it gets encapsulated with Transport, Network, and Data Link headers, understanding exactly which fields change at intermediate switches and routers.

docs.title: 🌐 Chapter 01: Internet Architecture & Network Core Switching
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text:
The Internet is a complex network of networks connecting billions of computing devices worldwide. Structurally, it is decomposed into two distinct realms: * The Network Edge: Hosts, end systems (computers, smartphones, IoT sensors, servers), and access networks (Ethernet, WiFi, cellular) that generate and consume data. * The Network Core: The interconnected mesh of packet switches, routers, and communication links that transport data from source to destination.

At the heart of the network core lies the fundamental question of how data moves across intermediate nodes. Historically and conceptually, this is solved by two competing paradigms: Circuit Switching (reserved, dedicated paths) and Packet Switching (dynamic, shared store-and-forward).

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Distinguish between Network Edge devices and Network Core devices. * Explain the inner workings of Circuit Switching through Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM) and Time Division Multiplexing (TDM). * Understand Packet Switching and why statistical multiplexing enables far greater user density than circuit switching. * Solve mathematical problems calculating file transmission times over TDM circuits. * Apply the Binomial Distribution formula to calculate the probability of link congestion when \(N\) bursty users share a packet-switched link.

docs.title: 3.1 Network Edge vs. Network Core
docs.text:
• End Systems (Hosts): Run application programs (e.g., Web browser, email client). Hosts sit strictly at the edge of the network.
  • Network Core: A mesh of routers and switches interconnected by communication links (optical fiber, copper wire, satellite). The core's sole job is to move data across intermediate hops toward its final destination.
  • Routing vs. Forwarding:
  • Routing (Decision): Network-wide process that uses routing algorithms (e.g., Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford) to determine the end-to-end optimal path across routers.
  • Forwarding / Switching (Action): Local per-router action that transfers a packet from an incoming interface link to the appropriate outgoing interface link based on the router's forwarding table.
Routing  = Decision Making (Global Algorithm -> Generates Routing Table)
Switching/Forwarding = Execution (Local Router Action -> Uses Table)

docs.title: 3.2 Circuit Switching: Dedicated Resource Allocation
docs.text:
In circuit switching, the resources (buffers, bandwidth) needed along a path between two communicating end systems are strictly reserved and dedicated for the entire duration of the communication session. * Guaranteed Bandwidth: Constant transmission speed, zero queuing delay. * Inefficiency: If a user pauses or does not transmit, the allocated bandwidth remains idle and cannot be utilized by other users. * Primary Use Case: Traditional Public Switched Telephone Networks (PSTN), legacy 2G/3G voice calls.

Circuit switching divides link capacity using two multiplexing techniques: 1. Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM): The frequency spectrum of a link is split into distinct narrow bands. Each call is allocated a dedicated frequency band for its entire duration (like radio stations). 2. Time Division Multiplexing (TDM): Time is divided into discrete, periodic frames of fixed duration. Each frame is subdivided into a fixed number of time slots. Each call is allocated a dedicated recurring time slot in every frame.

docs.title: 3.3 Packet Switching: Statistical Multiplexing & Store-and-Forward
docs.text: In packet switching, end-to-end data streams are divided into chunks of bits called packets. Packets share network links on-demand: * Store-and-Forward: A packet switch must receive the entire packet before it can begin transmitting the first bit onto the outbound link. * Statistical Multiplexing: Users transmit in bursts rather than continuously. Multiple users share the same channel dynamically without fixed reservations. * Queuing Delay & Packet Loss: If packets arrive at a router faster than the outbound link's transmission rate, they enter an output buffer (queue). If the buffer fills completely, arriving packets are dropped (packet loss).

docs.title: Circuit Switching Lifecycle:
docs.text:
1. Circuit Establishment: Signaling messages travel end-to-end to reserve frequency bands or time slots at every intermediate switch. (Introduces setup delay, e.g., 500 ms).
  2. Data Transfer: Data flows continuously with zero queuing delay.
  3. Circuit Teardown: Resources are released along all switches.

docs.title: Packet Switching Lifecycle:
docs.text:
1. Packetization: Application message is broken into packets at the edge.
  2. Hop-by-hop Transmission: Each router receives the entire packet, checks for errors, inspects the destination address in the header, and queues it for the outbound link.
  3. Store-and-Forward: Packet is transmitted onto the link at full link bandwidth \(R\).

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text:
• Circuit Switching Analogy (Reserved Train Carriage): You book an entire private train compartment from Dhaka to Chittagong. Even if you sleep and use only one seat, nobody else is allowed inside. Bandwidth is guaranteed, but space is wasted if idle.
  • Packet Switching Analogy (Highway Traffic): Thousands of cars and delivery trucks share the highway. When traffic is light, everyone drives at top speed. During peak rush hours, traffic jams (queues) form, and cars must wait.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation:
docs.text:
1. Allocated Bandwidth per TDM Slot: $\(\text{Bandwidth}_{\text{slot}} = \frac{\text{Total Link Bandwidth}}{\text{Number of Slots per Second}}\)$
  2. Transmission Time over Circuit: $\(\text{Time}_{\text{total}} = \text{Setup Time} + \frac{\text{File Size (bits)}}{\text{Bandwidth}_{\text{slot}}}\)$
  3. Binomial Probability of \(k\) active users among \(N\) total users (each active with probability \(p\)): $\(P(X = k) = \binom{N}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{N - k} = \frac{N!}{k!(N - k)!} p^k (1 - p)^{N - k}\)$

docs.title: Python Verification Script:
docs.text:
import math

def tdm_transmission_time(file_size_bits, link_rate_bps, num_slots, setup_time_s):
    slot_rate = link_rate_bps / num_slots
    tx_time = file_size_bits / slot_rate
    total_time = setup_time_s + tx_time
    return slot_rate, tx_time, total_time

def binomial_prob(n, k, p):
    comb = math.comb(n, k)
    return comb * (p ** k) * ((1 - p) ** (n - k))

def prob_more_than_k(n, k, p):
    return sum(binomial_prob(n, i, p) for i in range(k + 1, n + 1))

# Test Case matching UIU Class Lecture 03:
# Link: 1.536 Mbps, 24 slots/sec, File: 640,000 bits, Setup: 500 ms (0.5 s)
slot_bw, tx, total = tdm_transmission_time(640000, 1.536e6, 24, 0.5)
print(f"Slot Bandwidth: {slot_bw} bps | Tx Time: {tx} s | Total: {total} s")

# Test Case: 15 users, link supports 8 users simultaneously, active 20% of time
p_congestion = prob_more_than_k(15, 8, 0.20)
print(f"Probability of congestion (>8 users transmitting): {p_congestion:.6f}")

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Unit Confusion (b vs. B): Bandwidth is specified in bits per second (bps), while file sizes are often written in Bytes (B). Always multiply Bytes by 8 before calculating delays! (\(1\text{ Byte} = 8\text{ bits}\)). * Metric vs. Binary Prefixes: In Computer Networking, link speeds use metric multipliers: - \(1\text{ kbps} = 10^3\text{ bps}\) - \(1\text{ Mbps} = 10^6\text{ bps}\) - \(1\text{ Gbps} = 10^9\text{ bps}\) * Neglecting Circuit Setup Time: In circuit switching problems, do not forget to add the initial circuit establishment delay to the transmission time!

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From Class Lecture 03 Notes, Exercise 4)
docs.text:
Question: How long does it take to send a file of \(640,000\text{ bits}\) from Host A to Host B over a circuit-switched network? * All links are \(1.536\text{ Mbps}\) (\(1.536 \times 10^6\text{ bps}\)). * Each link uses TDM with \(24\text{ slots/second}\). * Circuit establishment takes \(500\text{ msec}\) (\(0.5\text{ s}\)).

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Find Allocated Bandwidth per Slot: $\(\text{Slot Bandwidth} = \frac{1.536 \times 10^6\text{ bps}}{24} = 64,000\text{ bps}\)$ 2. Calculate File Transmission Time: $\(\text{Tx Time} = \frac{640,000\text{ bits}}{64,000\text{ bps}} = 10\text{ seconds}\)$ 3. Add Circuit Establishment Delay: $\(\text{Total Time} = 10\text{ s} + 0.5\text{ s} = \mathbf{10.5\text{ seconds}}\)$

docs.title: 📝 Problem 2 (From Class Lecture 03 Notes, Exercise 6)
docs.text:
Question: Users share a link of capacity \(200\text{ Mbps}\). Each user requires \(25\text{ Mbps}\) when transmitting, but only transmits \(20\%\) of the time (\(p = 0.2\)). 1. When circuit switching is used, how many users can be supported? 2. If packet switching is used with \(15\text{ users}\), what is the probability that all 15 users transmit simultaneously? 3. What is the probability that more than 8 users transmit simultaneously?

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Circuit Switching User Capacity: $\(N_{cs} = \frac{\text{Total Capacity}}{\text{Per-User Rate}} = \frac{200\text{ Mbps}}{25\text{ Mbps}} = \mathbf{8\text{ users}}\)$ 2. Probability that all 15 users transmit at the same time: $\(P(X = 15) = (0.2)^{15} \approx \mathbf{3.28 \times 10^{-11}}\)$ 3. Probability that more than 8 users transmit simultaneously: Since the link can only serve up to 8 users simultaneously without queuing, having \(>8\) users active will cause queuing delay and potential packet drops: $\(P(X > 8) = \sum_{i=9}^{15} \binom{15}{i} (0.2)^i (1 - 0.2)^{15 - i} \approx \mathbf{0.000372} \ (0.037\%)\)$ Conclusion: In packet switching, 15 users can be supported with a negligible probability (\(<0.04\%\)) of queue overload, whereas circuit switching strictly limits support to only 8 users!

docs.title: Q1. Why does Packet Switching support more users than Circuit Switching?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Packet switching links have higher physical bandwidth.
  • [x] B) Most users transmit data in intermittent bursts, allowing statistical multiplexing of link capacity.
  • [ ] C) Packet switching eliminates propagation delay.
  • [ ] D) Packet switches do not require memory buffers. Explanation: Because user traffic is bursty, statistical multiplexing dynamically allocates capacity only to active users, supporting 2x to 3x more users than static reservations.

docs.title: Q2. In a TDM circuit with 10 slots per frame and a total link rate of 100 Mbps, what rate does an individual user experience?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) 100 Mbps continuously
  • [x] B) 10 Mbps effective continuous rate (or 100 Mbps during their 1/10th time slot)
  • [ ] C) 1 Gbps
  • [ ] D) 50 Mbps Explanation: \(100\text{ Mbps} / 10\text{ slots} = 10\text{ Mbps}\) dedicated bandwidth.

docs.title: Q3. In packet switching, if 1 Mbps link supports users who each require 100 kbps but are active only 10% of the time, how many simultaneous users can be supported versus circuit switching?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Same as circuit switching: 10 users
  • [x] B) Far more than 10 users — up to 35+ users with low congestion probability (Binomial probability analysis)
  • [ ] C) 100 users with guaranteed QoS
  • [ ] D) Exactly 10 users since link rate is fixed Explanation: Circuit switching hard-allocates bandwidth: 1 Mbps / 100 kbps = 10 users. Packet switching can serve far more because users are rarely all active simultaneously. With N=35 users each active 10% of the time, the probability all 35 transmit simultaneously is astronomically small.

docs.title: Q4. What is the fundamental difference between the network edge and the network core?
docs.text:
• [x] A) Edge contains end-systems (hosts) running applications; Core contains packet switches (routers) that forward data
  • [ ] B) Edge is faster than the core
  • [ ] C) Edge uses circuit switching; core uses packet switching
  • [ ] D) They are the same — edge and core are synonymous terms Explanation: The network edge (access network) hosts end-user devices (laptops, phones, servers). The network core is the mesh of interconnected packet switches and links that moves data from source to destination. No end-user applications run in the core.

docs.title: Q5. Which type of network uses store-and-forward transmission at every intermediate node?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Circuit-switched networks
  • [ ] B) Frequency Division Multiplexing networks
  • [x] C) Packet-switched networks
  • [ ] D) Time Division Multiplexing networks Explanation: In packet-switched networks, every router must receive the complete packet before it can begin forwarding it onto the next link. This is the store-and-forward principle. Circuit-switched networks create a dedicated end-to-end pipe — bits flow through without buffering at intermediate nodes.

docs.title: Q6. Why do ISPs (Internet Service Providers) at the same hierarchical level (Tier-1) connect directly via peering links rather than through a paying transit provider?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Legal requirements mandate peering between Tier-1 ISPs
  • [ ] B) Peering links are always faster than transit links
  • [x] C) Settlement-free peering eliminates transit costs — data flows between peers for free, reducing operational expenses
  • [ ] D) Tier-1 ISPs cannot purchase transit from anyone since they are at the top level Explanation: Tier-1 ISPs (e.g., AT&T, NTT) have global reach. By establishing settlement-free peering agreements, they exchange traffic directly without paying each other, significantly reducing costs compared to purchasing upstream transit bandwidth.

docs.title: Q7. What is a "Point of Presence" (PoP) in the context of ISP architecture?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) A special type of end-host in the access network
  • [x] B) A group of routers in a provider's network where customer ISPs can connect to the provider's backbone
  • [ ] C) The physical location of a DNS root server
  • [ ] D) The geographic center of an Autonomous System Explanation: A PoP (Point of Presence) is a geographic location where a provider ISP has routers that lower-level ISPs can connect into. It is the entry point into an ISP's backbone network.

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Network Edge: End systems (PCs, phones, servers) running distributed applications.
  • Network Core: Mesh of packet switches (routers) forwarding packets across hops.
  • Circuit Switching: Dedicated reservation (FDM/TDM). Zero queuing delay, guaranteed throughput, but bandwidth wasted during silence periods.
  • Packet Switching: On-demand store-and-forward sharing. High resource utilization, supports many bursty users, but introduces queuing delay and packet loss risk.
  • Capacity Formula: $\(N_{cs} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{Link Capacity}}{\text{User Rate}} \right\rfloor\)$

docs.title: ⏱️ Chapter 02: Delay, Loss, and Throughput in Packet-Switched Networks
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: When a packet travels from a source host, across intermediate network routers, to a destination host, it suffers from several distinct types of delay at each node along its path. Understanding the mathematical breakdown of nodal delay, the conditions under which packet loss occurs, and how bottleneck links limit end-to-end throughput is essential for analyzing network performance and designing high-efficiency transport protocols.

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Identify and calculate the four fundamental components of Total Nodal Delay: Processing, Queuing, Transmission, and Propagation delay. * Understand the intuitive physics of networking through the classic Caravan Analogy. * Differentiate between delays dependent on the router hardware versus those dependent on the physical transmission medium. * Calculate end-to-end multi-hop delays across heterogenous transmission links. * Compute the queuing delay for an arriving packet based on the current queue depth. * Identify the bottleneck link and calculate maximum end-to-end effective throughput.

docs.title: 3.1 The 4 Components of Nodal Delay
docs.text:
At every packet switch (router), a packet experiences four distinct delays:

\[d_{\text{nodal}} = d_{\text{proc}} + d_{\text{que}} + d_{\text{trans}} + d_{\text{prop}}\] 
┌──────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐
│  Processing  │ ──> │   Queuing   │ ──> │  Transmission  │ ──> │  Propagation   │
│ Delay (dproc)│     │ Delay (dque)│     │  Delay (dtrans)│     │ Delay (dprop)  │
└──────────────┘     └─────────────┘     └────────────────┘     └────────────────┘
 Router CPU check     Buffer wait time    Push bits to wire      Flight time over wire
 (Header / Checksum)  (Function of queue) L / R (Link Rate)      d / s (Speed of light)
  1. Nodal Processing Delay (\(d_{\text{proc}}\)):
  2. Time required by the router CPU to inspect the packet header, verify the checksum for bit errors, and determine the outbound interface link from its routing table.
  3. Property: Typically microseconds or less; depends on router hardware speed.
  4. Queuing Delay (\(d_{\text{que}}\)):
  5. Time the packet waits in the output buffer queue before it can begin transmission.
  6. Property: Variable! Depends on network traffic intensity. If \(n\) packets are ahead in the queue: $\(d_{\text{que}} = n \times \frac{L}{R}\)$
  7. Transmission Delay (\(d_{\text{trans}}\)):
  8. Time required to push (pump) all of the packet's bits onto the physical link.
  9. Formula: $\(d_{\text{trans}} = \frac{L}{R}\)$ where \(L\) is the packet length in bits, and \(R\) is the link transmission rate in bits/sec (bps).
  10. Property: Dependent strictly on packet size and router interface link speed; independent of geographical distance!
  11. Propagation Delay (\(d_{\text{prop}}\)):
  12. Time required for a single bit to physically travel from the beginning of the link to the destination router across the physical medium (fiber optic, copper, air).
  13. Formula: $\(d_{\text{prop}} = \frac{d}{s}\)$ where \(d\) is the link length (distance in meters), and \(s\) is the propagation speed in the medium (\(s \approx 2 \times 10^8\text{ to } 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\)).
  14. Property: Dependent strictly on distance and physical medium; independent of packet size and link bandwidth!

docs.title: 3.2 The Caravan Analogy
docs.text: Consider a caravan of 10 cars (representing 10 bits of a packet) traveling down a 100 km highway between two toll booths (representing routers): * Toll Booth Service Time (Transmission Delay): The toll collector takes 12 seconds to service each car and release it onto the highway. Total time to service all 10 cars = \(10 \times 12\text{ s} = 120\text{ seconds}\) (\(d_{\text{trans}}\)). * Highway Travel Time (Propagation Delay): Once released, each car cruises at \(100\text{ km/h}\). The travel time over \(100\text{ km}\) = \(1\text{ hour}\) (\(d_{\text{prop}}\)). * Store-and-Forward Rule: The caravan cannot proceed past the second toll booth until the entire caravan of 10 cars has arrived and assembled!

docs.title: 3.3 Throughput & Bottleneck Links
docs.text:
• Throughput: The rate (bits per unit time, e.g., bps) at which bits are transferred from sender to receiver.
  • Bottleneck Link: The link on the end-to-end path that provides the minimum transmission capacity: $\(\text{Throughput} = \min(R_1, R_2, \dots, R_N)\)$
  • If a backbone link of \(R_{\text{shared}}\) is shared equally among \(M\) active connections, each user gets \(\frac{R_{\text{shared}}}{M}\).

docs.title: 4.1 Packet Delay Pipeline at a Router
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Packet as Arriving Packet
    participant Buffer as Router Queue
    participant Engine as Router CPU
    participant Line as Physical Wire

    Packet->>Engine: Arrives at interface -> d_proc (Header Check)
    Engine->>Buffer: Enters output buffer -> d_que (Waits for prior packets)
    Buffer->>Line: Pushed bit-by-bit onto wire -> d_trans = L / R
    Line->>Line: Electromagnetic signal travels -> d_prop = d / s

docs.title: 4.2 Bottleneck Link Pipeline
docs.text:
[Sender Host] === R1 (100 Mbps) ===> [Router] === R2 (10 Mbps) ===> [Router] === R3 (1 Gbps) ===> [Receiver Host]
                                                ▲
                                                │ Bottleneck Link!
                                                └─ Throughput = min(100, 10, 1000) = 10 Mbps

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step Multi-Hop Delay Calculation
docs.text: For a path with \(N\) links and \(N-1\) intermediate routers: 1. Source Host: Computes \(d_{\text{trans1}} = \frac{L}{R_1}\). (Note: hosts typically have negligible \(d_{\text{proc}}\) and \(d_{\text{que}}\) for outbound traffic). 2. Link 1: Propagates signal \(d_{\text{prop1}} = \frac{d_1}{s}\). 3. Router 1: - Incurs processing delay \(d_{\text{proc1}}\). - Incurs queuing delay \(d_{\text{que1}}\) (if other packets are in buffer). - Incurs transmission delay \(d_{\text{trans2}} = \frac{L}{R_2}\). 4. Intermediate Links: Repeats for each intermediate hop. 5. Destination Host: Receives the final bit; total delay is the sum of all components: $\(d_{\text{end-to-end}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( \frac{L}{R_i} + \frac{d_i}{s_i} \right) + \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} (d_{\text{proc}, j} + d_{\text{que}, j})\)$

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text:
• Water Pipe Network:
  • Pumping 100 liters of water through a funnel into a hose = Transmission delay (volume / pump speed).
  • The time the water droplets take to travel 50 meters through the garden hose to wet the flowers = Propagation delay (distance / water velocity).
  • Even with a massive fire hose at the source and destination, if there is a tiny 1-cm diameter connector in the middle, water flows at the rate of that tiny connector (Bottleneck link).

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python Calculation Engine)
docs.text:
class NetworkPath:
    def __init__(self, packet_size_bytes, prop_speed=3e8):
        self.L_bits = packet_size_bytes * 8
        self.prop_speed = prop_speed
        self.hops = []

    def add_hop(self, distance_meters, bandwidth_bps, d_proc_s=0.0, queue_packets=0):
        self.hops.append({
            'd': distance_meters,
            'R': bandwidth_bps,
            'd_proc': d_proc_s,
            'q': queue_packets
        })

    def calculate_total_delay(self):
        total_dtrans = 0
        total_dprop = 0
        total_dproc = 0
        total_dque = 0

        for i, hop in enumerate(self.hops):
            # Transmission delay on this link
            d_trans = self.L_bits / hop['R']
            # Propagation delay on this link
            d_prop = hop['d'] / self.prop_speed
            # Queuing delay if queue exists
            d_que = hop['q'] * (self.L_bits / hop['R'])
            # Processing delay at this hop (only for routers, hop 0 is sender)
            d_proc = hop['d_proc']

            total_dtrans += d_trans
            total_dprop += d_prop
            total_dproc += d_proc
            total_dque += d_que

        end_to_end = total_dtrans + total_dprop + total_dproc + total_dque
        bottleneck_bw = min(hop['R'] for hop in self.hops)

        return {
            'end_to_end_delay_ms': end_to_end * 1000,
            'transmission_delay_ms': total_dtrans * 1000,
            'propagation_delay_ms': total_dprop * 1000,
            'queuing_delay_ms': total_dque * 1000,
            'processing_delay_ms': total_dproc * 1000,
            'bottleneck_throughput_mbps': bottleneck_bw / 1e6
        }

# Verify UIU Class Note 1, Page 7 (Content 1: 8 Problem):
# Packet L = 16,000 bits. 3 Links:
# Link 1: 2 km, 1000 Mbps
# Link 2: 500 km, 10 Mbps
# Link 3: 3 km, 100 Mbps
path = NetworkPath(packet_size_bytes=16000//8, prop_speed=3e8)
path.add_hop(distance_meters=2000, bandwidth_bps=1000e6)
path.add_hop(distance_meters=500e3, bandwidth_bps=10e6)
path.add_hop(distance_meters=3000, bandwidth_bps=100e6)

res = path.calculate_total_delay()
print("End-to-End Delay:", res['end_to_end_delay_ms'], "ms")
print("Bottleneck Throughput:", res['bottleneck_throughput_mbps'], "Mbps")

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!CAUTION] 1. Applying Processing Delay at the Sender: A sender host does not experience router processing delay \(d_{\text{proc}}\) for outbound traffic; \(d_{\text{proc}}\) occurs at intermediate routers examining incoming headers! 2. Confusing Bandwidth with Signal Speed: A \(10\text{ Gbps}\) fiber link does NOT send bits faster across the distance than a \(10\text{ Mbps}\) fiber link! Both transmit electromagnetic waves at the same physical speed of light (\(s \approx 2 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\)). Higher bandwidth simply means bits are pushed closer together in time (\(d_{\text{trans}} = L/R\) is shorter). 3. Fractional Packets in Queuing: If a question states that 200 full packets and half of another packet are in the queue, \(n = 200.5\) packets!

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 7: Content 1.8)
docs.text:
Question: A packet of size \(L = 16,000\text{ bits}\) is sent from Host A to Host B across 3 links separated by 2 routers. Propagation speed \(s = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\). Neglect queuing and processing delays. * Link 1: \(d_1 = 2\text{ km}\), \(R_1 = 1000\text{ Mbps}\) * Link 2: \(d_2 = 500\text{ km}\), \(R_2 = 10\text{ Mbps}\) * Link 3: \(d_3 = 3\text{ km}\), \(R_3 = 100\text{ Mbps}\) Calculate the total end-to-end delay.

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Link 1 Delay: $\(d_{\text{trans1}} = \frac{16,000}{1000 \times 10^6} = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s} = 0.016\text{ ms}\)$ $\(d_{\text{prop1}} = \frac{2 \times 10^3}{3 \times 10^8} = 6.67 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s} = 0.00667\text{ ms}\)$ 2. Link 2 Delay: $\(d_{\text{trans2}} = \frac{16,000}{10 \times 10^6} = 1.6 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} = 1.6\text{ ms}\)$ $\(d_{\text{prop2}} = \frac{500 \times 10^3}{3 \times 10^8} = 1.667 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} = 1.667\text{ ms}\)$ 3. Link 3 Delay: $\(d_{\text{trans3}} = \frac{16,000}{100 \times 10^6} = 1.6 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s} = 0.16\text{ ms}\)$ $\(d_{\text{prop3}} = \frac{3 \times 10^3}{3 \times 10^8} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s} = 0.010\text{ ms}\)$ 4. End-to-End Total Delay: $\(d_{\text{total}} = (0.016 + 0.00667) + (1.6 + 1.667) + (0.16 + 0.010) = \mathbf{3.45967\text{ ms}}\)$

docs.title: 📝 Problem 2 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 8: Q.4)
docs.text:
Question: A packet arrives at a router buffer where 200 packets and half of another packet are currently queued awaiting transmission. Packet size \(L = 64\text{ Bytes}\), link rate \(R = 10\text{ Mbps}\). What is the queuing delay experienced by this arriving packet?

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Number of packets ahead in queue: $\(n = 200 + 0.5 = 200.5\text{ packets}\)$ 2. Transmission time per packet: $\(\frac{L}{R} = \frac{64 \times 8\text{ bits}}{10 \times 10^6\text{ bps}} = \frac{512}{10^7} = 5.12 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s} = 0.0512\text{ ms}\)$ 3. Queuing Delay (\(d_{\text{que}}\)): $\(d_{\text{que}} = 200.5 \times \frac{L}{R} = 200.5 \times (5.12 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s}) = 0.0102656\text{ s} = \mathbf{10.2656\text{ ms}}\)$

docs.title: 📝 Problem 3 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 10: Q.253(c))
docs.text:
Question: A server transmits a file of size \(1\text{ Gb}\) (\(1 \times 10^9\text{ bits}\)). The server link has rate \(R_s = 200\text{ Mbps}\), the client link has rate \(R_c = 50\text{ Mbps}\). They are connected across a core network link of \(100\text{ Mbps}\) that is shared equally among \(25\text{ users}\). What is the transmission time of the file?

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Calculate per-user capacity on the shared core link: $\(R_{\text{shared-per-user}} = \frac{100\text{ Mbps}}{25} = 4\text{ Mbps}\)$ 2. Identify the Bottleneck Link Capacity: $\(R_{\min} = \min(R_s, R_{\text{shared-per-user}}, R_c) = \min(200\text{ Mbps}, 4\text{ Mbps}, 50\text{ Mbps}) = \mathbf{4\text{ Mbps}}\)$ 3. Calculate File Transmission Time: $\(\text{Tx Time} = \frac{L}{R_{\min}} = \frac{1 \times 10^9\text{ bits}}{4 \times 10^6\text{ bps}} = \mathbf{250\text{ seconds}}\)$

docs.title: Q1. If you double the physical length of a cable without changing bandwidth or packet size, which delay doubles?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Transmission delay (\(d_{\text{trans}}\))
  • [x] B) Propagation delay (\(d_{\text{prop}}\))
  • [ ] C) Processing delay (\(d_{\text{proc}}\))
  • [ ] D) Queuing delay (\(d_{\text{que}}\)) Explanation: \(d_{\text{prop}} = d / s\). Doubling distance \(d\) directly doubles propagation delay.

docs.title: Q2. A link has bandwidth \(R = 100\text{ Mbps}\). An arriving packet has length \(L = 1250\text{ Bytes}\). What is \(d_{\text{trans}}\)?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) \(0.1\text{ ms}\)
  • [x] B) \(0.1\text{ ms}\) (\(100\text{ }\mu\text{s}\))
  • [ ] C) \(12.5\text{ ms}\)
  • [ ] D) \(1\text{ ms}\) Explanation: \(L = 1250 \times 8 = 10,000\text{ bits}\). \(d_{\text{trans}} = 10,000 / (100 \times 10^6) = 10^{-4}\text{ s} = 0.1\text{ ms} = 100\text{ }\mu\text{s}\).

docs.title: Q3. For a 150 km fiber link with propagation speed \(s = 2 \times 10^8\) m/s and a 1 Gbps link rate sending a 12,000-bit packet, which delay type dominates?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Transmission delay dominates: \(d_{\text{trans}} = 12,000 / 10^9 = 12\ \mu\text{s}\) vs \(d_{\text{prop}} = 0.75\ \text{ms}\)
  • [x] B) Propagation delay dominates: \(d_{\text{prop}} = (150 \times 10^3) / (2 \times 10^8) = 0.75\ \text{ms}\) vs \(d_{\text{trans}} = 12\ \mu\text{s}\)
  • [ ] C) They are approximately equal
  • [ ] D) Processing delay dominates over both Explanation: \(d_{\text{trans}} = 12,000 / (10^9) = 12\ \mu\text{s}\). \(d_{\text{prop}} = 150,000 / (2 \times 10^8) = 0.75\ \text{ms} = 750\ \mu\text{s}\). Propagation delay is 62.5× larger than transmission delay on this long-distance high-bandwidth link.

docs.title: Q3. The traffic intensity \(\rho = La/R\). What happens as \(\rho \to 1\)?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Queuing delay approaches zero
  • [ ] B) Queuing delay equals exactly one transmission delay \(L/R\)
  • [x] C) Average queuing delay approaches infinity — the queue grows without bound
  • [ ] D) Packet loss stops occurring Explanation: Traffic intensity \(\rho = La/R\) where \(L\) = packet length, \(a\) = packet arrival rate, \(R\) = link bandwidth. When \(\rho \geq 1\), packets arrive faster than they can be served. The queue grows unboundedly and average queuing delay \(\to \infty\). This is why \(\rho < 1\) is a fundamental design requirement.

docs.title: Q4. What is the effective end-to-end throughput for a file transfer where \(R_s = 500\ \text{Mbps}\), \(R_c = 20\ \text{Mbps}\), and 10 other flows share a 100 Mbps core link?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) \(500\ \text{Mbps}\) (server capacity)
  • [x] B) \(10\ \text{Mbps}\) (shared core link bottleneck: \(100/10 = 10\ \text{Mbps per flow}\))
  • [ ] C) \(20\ \text{Mbps}\) (client capacity)
  • [ ] D) \(1\ \text{Gbps}\) (maximum theoretical) Explanation: Core link: \(100\ \text{Mbps} \div 10\ \text{flows} = 10\ \text{Mbps per flow}\). Bottleneck \(= \min(500, 10, 20) = \mathbf{10\ \text{Mbps}}\). The shared core link is the bottleneck, not the server or client access link.

docs.title: Q5. Packet loss at a router occurs when:
docs.text:
• [ ] A) The propagation delay exceeds 1 second
  • [ ] B) The link bandwidth is greater than 1 Gbps
  • [x] C) The output buffer is completely full and a new packet arrives
  • [ ] D) The processing delay exceeds the queuing delay Explanation: Every router has a finite output buffer (queue). When the queue is 100% full and a new packet arrives, the router has no space to store it and drops the packet. This is called packet loss. The packet is simply discarded — no notification to the sender (TCP detects loss and retransmits; UDP does not).

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text: Delay Component Formula Dependent On Hardware / Physics Processing (\(d_{\text{proc}}\)) Fixed by CPU Router processor, header complexity Router Hardware Queuing (\(d_{\text{que}}\)) \(n \times (L / R)\) Buffer congestion, arrival traffic Dynamic Traffic Load Transmission (\(d_{\text{trans}}\)) \(L / R\) Packet length (\(L\)), Link Bandwidth (\(R\)) Network Interface Speed Propagation (\(d_{\text{prop}}\)) \(d / s\) Distance (\(d\)), Medium speed (\(s\)) Physical Medium Physics Bottleneck Throughput \(\min(R_1, \dots, R_N)\) Weakest link on end-to-end path Topology Constrained

docs.title: 📦 Chapter 03: Layered Architecture, Encapsulation, and Addressing
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: Computer networks are extraordinarily complex systems comprising diverse hardware, communication media, operating systems, and distributed applications. To manage this immense complexity, network designers organize network protocols into hierarchical layers. Each layer provides specific services to the layer above it while relying on the services of the layer below. As application data travels down the protocol stack, it undergoes encapsulation (adding headers/trailers) and, at the receiving end, decapsulation.

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Explain the benefits of layering: Modularity, Ease of Troubleshooting, and Function Reuse. * Compare the OSI 7-Layer Reference Model with the TCP/IP 5-Layer Model. * Distinguish the protocol stack depth processed by Hubs (Layer 1), Switches (Layer 2), and Routers (Layer 3). * Trace the encapsulation of application data into Transport segments, Network datagrams, and Data Link frames. * Understand the three distinct levels of addressing: Process-to-Process (Port), Host-to-Host (IP), and Hop-to-Hop (MAC). * Calculate segment count, maximum payload, and overhead percentages under varying Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) constraints.

docs.title: 3.1 Why Layering?
docs.text:
1. Modularity: Decomposes a monolithic networking system into manageable, independent functional modules.
  2. Ease of Troubleshooting: If a link cable breaks, engineers troubleshoot Layer 1 without modifying web browser application code (Layer 5).
  3. Function Reuse (Framework): Multiple diverse applications (HTTP, FTP, SMTP) reuse the same underlying Transport (TCP/UDP) and Network (IP) layers.

docs.title: 3.3 Addressing at Each Layer
docs.text: Level Name Scope & Purpose Does it change across hops? Layer 4 Port Number (16-bit) Process-to-Process: Identifies the specific application process running on the host (e.g., Port 80 HTTP, Port 53 DNS). ❌ No (Remains static end-to-end, unless NAT intervenes) Layer 3 IP Address (32-bit IPv4) Host-to-Host: Globally identifies the source host and destination host across the global Internet. ❌ No (Remains constant from source to destination) Layer 2 MAC Address (48-bit) Hop-to-Hop: Identifies physical interfaces on the immediate local link. ✅ YES! (Rewritten at every intermediate router interface!)

docs.title: 3.4 Devices Operating at Different Layers
docs.text:
• Hub (Layer 1): Physical-layer repeater. Receives raw bits on one port and blindly electrical-broadcasts them to all other ports. Does not read frames or IP packets.
  • Switch (Layer 2): Data link device. Inspects incoming frames up to the Layer 2 MAC header. Forwards frames selectively to target devices based on MAC tables.
  • Router (Layer 3): Network device. Inspects packets up to the Layer 3 IP header. Strips the incoming Layer 2 frame header, inspects the destination IP address, consults its routing table, decrements TTL, and encapsulates the packet into a brand-new Layer 2 frame for the next hop.

docs.title: 4.1 Encapsulation and Data Units
docs.text:
Application Layer:    [ Application Message M: "Hello" ]
                               │
Transport Layer:      [ H_T (Port) | M ]                  ==> Segment
                               │
Network Layer:        [ H_N (IP)   | H_T | M ]            ==> Datagram / Packet
                               │
Data Link Layer:      [ H_D (MAC)  | H_N | H_T | M | T_D ]==> Frame (Header + CRC Trailer)
                               │
Physical Layer:       0 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 1 1 1 ...         ==> Signals / Bits

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step Traversal Walkthrough
docs.text:
Tracing a packet from Sender (IP: 100, MAC: sen, Port: c) to Receiver (IP: 200, MAC: Rec, Port: z) via Router (MAC: ROU):

  1. At Sender Host:
  2. Application generates message "Hello".
  3. Transport layer prepends port header: [Src: c | Dst: z | "Hello"].
  4. Network layer prepends IP header: [Src: 100 | Dst: 200 | PortHeader | "Hello"].
  5. Data link layer prepends MAC header: [Src: sen | Dst: ROU | IPHeader | PortHeader | "Hello"].
  6. On Physical Wire 1: Transmitted as physical electromagnetic bits to the Router.
  7. At Intermediate Router:
  8. Layer 1 receives bits \(\to\) delivers to Layer 2.
  9. Layer 2 checks Dst: ROU. Since it matches the router's interface MAC, it strips the MAC header and passes the IP datagram to Layer 3.
  10. Layer 3 inspects Dst: 200. Consults routing table: Next hop is Host B directly.
  11. Layer 3 passes the datagram back down to Layer 2.
  12. Crucial Step: Layer 2 constructs a new frame with: [Src: ROU | Dst: Rec | SrcIP: 100 | DstIP: 200 | PortHeader | "Hello"].
  13. At Receiver Host:
  14. Layer 2 matches Dst: Rec, strips MAC header.
  15. Layer 3 matches Dst: 200, strips IP header.
  16. Layer 4 matches Dst Port: z (e.g., WhatsApp process), delivers clean message "Hello" to the application!

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example (Postal Mail Analogy)
docs.text:
• Application Data: Ashik writes a confidential handwritten letter to Khan.
  • Transport Layer (Envelope): Ashik puts the letter in an envelope and writes Khan’s department/room number (Port).
  • Network Layer (Postal Address): He writes Khan’s building street address and city (IP Address).
  • Data Link Layer (Mail Truck Hops): The envelope is put into a delivery pouch tagged from Ashik's local post office to the Central Sorting Hub (Hop 1 MAC). At the sorting hub, it is moved to another truck tagged to Khan’s regional depot (Hop 2 MAC). The truck tags change at every facility, but the recipient's name and city never change!

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Segmentation & Overhead Calculation)
docs.text:
import math

def calculate_segmentation(data_size_bytes, mtu_bytes, transport_h=20, network_h=20, link_h=14, link_t=4):
    link_overhead_per_frame = link_h + link_t       # 14 + 4 = 18 bytes
    total_header_per_segment = transport_h + network_h + link_overhead_per_frame # 20 + 20 + 18 = 58 bytes

    # Maximum application payload per physical frame:
    max_payload = mtu_bytes - total_header_per_segment
    num_segments = math.ceil(data_size_bytes / max_payload)

    # Calculate overhead
    total_overhead = num_segments * total_header_per_segment
    total_transmitted = data_size_bytes + total_overhead
    overhead_percentage = (total_overhead / total_transmitted) * 100

    return {
        'max_payload_per_segment': max_payload,
        'num_segments': num_segments,
        'overhead_per_segment': total_header_per_segment,
        'total_overhead_bytes': total_overhead,
        'overhead_percentage': round(overhead_percentage, 2)
    }

# Test Case from CN Class Note 1, Page 15:
# Data = 4000 B, Transport = 20 B, Network = 20 B, DataLink = 14 B header + 4 B trailer = 18 B.
# Case 1: MTU = 1518 Bytes
case1 = calculate_segmentation(4000, 1518)
print("Case 1 (MTU 1518):", case1)

# Case 2: MTU = 1200 Bytes
case2 = calculate_segmentation(4000, 1200)
print("Case 2 (MTU 1200):", case2)

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Assuming IP addresses change at routers: IP addresses (\(100 \to 200\)) remain strictly constant across all standard routers from source to destination. Only MAC addresses are rewritten at each hop! (The only exception is NAT routers, studied in Module 05). * Forgetting the Frame Trailer: Ethernet Data Link frames have both a 14-byte Header and a 4-byte CRC Trailer, giving a total link layer overhead of \(18\text{ Bytes}\).

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 15 & Midterm 261 Q1(c))
docs.text:
Question: Host A wants to send an application data message of size \(4,000\text{ Bytes}\) to Host B. * Application layer message: \(4,000\text{ Bytes}\). * Transport layer header (\(H_T\)): \(20\text{ Bytes}\). * Network layer header (\(H_N\)): \(20\text{ Bytes}\). * Data link layer: Header (\(H_D\)) = \(14\text{ Bytes}\), Trailer (\(T_D\)) = \(4\text{ Bytes}\). 1. If the maximum frame capacity (MTU) is \(1,518\text{ Bytes}\), find the number of segments required and total overhead bytes. 2. If the path capacity changes such that the maximum frame size is reduced to \(1,200\text{ Bytes}\), how many segments are required and what is the new total overhead?

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Total Overhead per Segment: $\(\text{Overhead} = H_D + H_N + H_T + T_D = 14 + 20 + 20 + 4 = \mathbf{58\text{ Bytes}}\)$ 2. Case 1 (Frame Capacity = \(1,518\text{ Bytes}\)): * Maximum original data payload per segment: $\(\text{Payload}_{\max} = 1518 - 58 = 1460\text{ Bytes}\)$ * Number of segments: $\(\text{Segments} = \left\lceil \frac{4000}{1460} \right\rceil = \lceil 2.74 \rceil = \mathbf{3\text{ segments}}\)$ (Breakdown: Segment 1 = 1460 B, Segment 2 = 1460 B, Segment 3 = 1080 B) * Total overhead added: $\(\text{Total Overhead} = 3 \times 58\text{ Bytes} = \mathbf{174\text{ Bytes}}\)$ 3. Case 2 (Frame Capacity = \(1,200\text{ Bytes}\)): * Maximum original data payload per segment: $\(\text{Payload}_{\max} = 1200 - 58 = 1142\text{ Bytes}\)$ * Number of segments: $\(\text{Segments} = \left\lceil \frac{4000}{1142} \right\rceil = \lceil 3.50 \rceil = \mathbf{4\text{ segments}}\)$ * Total overhead added: $\(\text{Total Overhead} = 4 \times 58\text{ Bytes} = \mathbf{232\text{ Bytes}}\)$

docs.title: Q1. When a router forwards a packet from one Ethernet link to another, which fields change?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Source IP and Destination IP
  • [ ] B) Source Port and Destination Port
  • [x] C) Source MAC and Destination MAC
  • [ ] D) Application Payload Explanation: Standard routers inspect IP headers to make forwarding decisions, decrement TTL, and encapsulate the packet in a new Data Link frame with the router's outbound interface MAC as Source MAC and the next-hop interface MAC as Destination MAC.

docs.title: Q2. A Layer 2 Switch inspects packet headers up to which layer?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Physical (Layer 1) only
  • [x] B) Data Link (Layer 2)
  • [ ] C) Network (Layer 3)
  • [ ] D) Transport (Layer 4) Explanation: Switches operate at Layer 2 (Data Link), reading destination MAC addresses to switch frames to appropriate switch ports.

docs.title: Q3. When a router forwards an IP datagram between two Ethernet segments, which layers does it process?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) All 7 layers (Application through Physical)
  • [ ] B) Only the Physical layer (Layer 1)
  • [x] C) Layers 1 and 2 (Physical + Data Link) to receive the frame, then Layer 3 (Network) to route and forward
  • [ ] D) Only Layer 3 (Network layer) Explanation: A router is a Layer 3 device. It processes from Physical (L1) → Data Link (L2) to receive the incoming frame, strips the L2 header to extract the IP datagram, reads the L3 IP header to determine the forwarding path, then encapsulates in a new L2 frame for the outgoing interface. It does NOT process L4-L7.

docs.title: Q4. What is the correct term for the data unit at each layer when moving top-down through the Internet protocol stack?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Message → Datagram → Segment → Frame → Bit
  • [x] B) Message → Segment → Datagram → Frame → Bit
  • [ ] C) Frame → Datagram → Segment → Message → Bit
  • [ ] D) Bit → Frame → Segment → Datagram → Message Explanation: Application layer creates a Message. Transport layer adds its header → Segment (TCP) or Datagram (UDP). Network layer adds IP header → Datagram. Link layer adds frame header/trailer → Frame. Physical layer transmits → Bits.

docs.title: Q5. Why does the Internet model have only 5 layers while the OSI reference model has 7?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) The Internet model is older and hasn't been updated
  • [x] B) The Internet model merges Presentation (encryption/compression) and Session (connection management) into the Application layer, since these are handled by applications as needed
  • [ ] C) OSI adds 2 extra layers for security reasons
  • [ ] D) The Internet model excludes the Physical layer entirely Explanation: The OSI model (1984) added the Presentation Layer (data encoding, encryption, compression) and Session Layer (session management, synchronization) as explicit separate layers. In the Internet model, these functions are implemented inside Application layer protocols as needed (e.g., TLS/SSL handles encryption, HTTP handles session state via cookies), so they aren't formalized as separate layers.

docs.title: Q6. What is the purpose of a "trailer" in a Data Link layer frame, and which error-detection value is typically stored there?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) The trailer stores routing information for the next hop
  • [x] B) The trailer stores the CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) checksum for error detection on the link
  • [ ] C) The trailer contains the destination MAC address
  • [ ] D) The trailer is always empty and exists only for byte alignment Explanation: The Ethernet frame trailer contains the FCS (Frame Check Sequence) — typically a 4-byte CRC-32 value. The receiver recomputes the CRC over the received frame and compares it with the FCS. A mismatch indicates a bit error occurred on the link, and the frame is silently dropped (the sender's higher-layer protocol handles retransmission).

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• OSI 7 Layers: Physical \(\to\) Data Link \(\to\) Network \(\to\) Transport \(\to\) Session \(\to\) Presentation \(\to\) Application.
  • TCP/IP 5 Layers: Physical \(\to\) Data Link \(\to\) Network \(\to\) Transport \(\to\) Application.
  • Data Unit Names:
  • Transport Layer \(\to\) Segment
  • Network Layer \(\to\) Datagram / Packet
  • Data Link Layer \(\to\) Frame
  • Physical Layer \(\to\) Bits
  • Addressing Summary:
  • Port (16-bit) = Process on Host
  • IP (32-bit) = Host on Internet
  • MAC (48-bit) = Interface on Local Link

docs.title: 🔐 Module 02: Network Security Fundamentals
docs.text: Welcome to Module 02: Network Security Fundamentals. The Internet was originally conceived in an academic environment among mutually trusting researchers. As a result, security was not built into core IP protocols from inception. This module covers the foundational principles of the CIA Triad, cryptographic techniques to secure communications, the anatomy of major network attacks (Sniffing, Spoofing, and DDoS), and baseline defense mechanisms such as firewalls.

docs.title: 🎯 Key Competencies Acquired
docs.text: By completing this module, you will be able to: 1. Formulate network security requirements using the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) triad. 2. Differentiate between encryption (achieving Confidentiality) and digital signatures/hashes (achieving Integrity). 3. Trace how a packet sniffer intercepts unencrypted traffic on shared media. 4. Explain how IP address spoofing bypasses simple authentication mechanisms. 5. Contrast localized single-source DoS attacks with botnet-orchestrated Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) floods.

docs.title: 🛡️ Chapter 01: The CIA Triad and Cryptographic Foundations
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: In any distributed computing environment where data traverses untrusted public infrastructure, ensuring security is paramount. The entire discipline of information and network security rests upon a foundational three-pillar framework known as the CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. To enforce these properties, modern networking utilizes cryptographic primitives including symmetric and asymmetric encryption, cryptographic hashes, and digital signatures.

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Define and contrast the three pillars of the CIA Triad. * Explain how Encryption and Decryption provide message Confidentiality. * Demonstrate the mathematical mechanics of classical substitution ciphers (e.g., Caesar Cipher). * Understand how Cryptographic Hashes and Digital Signatures guarantee message Integrity and non-repudiation. * Distinguish between symmetric-key cryptography (shared secret) and public-key cryptography (public/private key pairs).

docs.title: 3.1 The CIA Triad
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────┐
             │    C: Confidentiality   │
             │   (Only sender/receiver │
             │    can understand text) │
             └────────────┬────────────┘
                          │
            ▲             │             ▲
           ╱ ╲            ▼            ╱ ╲
          ╱   ╲                       ╱   ╲
         ╱     ╲                     ╱     ╲
┌───────┴───────┴───────┐   ┌───────┴───────┴───────┐
│      I: Integrity     │   │    A: Availability    │
│  (Data not altered    │───│ (Services accessible  │
│   in transit)         │   │  to legitimate users) │
└───────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────┘
  1. Confidentiality:
  2. Definition: Ensures that only the intended sender and receiver can understand the contents of the transmitted message. An eavesdropper who intercepts the transmission should only see unintelligible ciphertext.
  3. Enforced By: Encryption (Plaintext \(\to\) Ciphertext) and Decryption (Ciphertext \(\to\) Plaintext).
  4. Integrity:
  5. Definition: Ensures that the message is not altered, tampered with, or injected with malicious content while in transit from source to destination.
  6. Enforced By: Cryptographic Hashes (SHA-256), Message Authentication Codes (MAC), and Digital Signatures.
  7. Availability:
  8. Definition: Ensures that network services, servers, and bandwidth remain accessible and responsive to legitimate users at all times.
  9. Threatened By: Denial-of-Service (DoS) and Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks.

docs.title: 1. Caesar Cipher (Classical Substitution):
docs.text:
The simplest historic encryption algorithm shifts every letter of the alphabet forward by a fixed key offset \(K\) (modulo 26): $\(C = (P + K) \pmod{26}\)$ $\(P = (C - K) \pmod{26}\)$

Example from Class Note 1 (Page 17): Key \(K = +3\) $\(\text{Plaintext: } \mathbf{H \ E \ L \ L \ O}\)$ - \(H \to K\) - \(E \to H\) - \(L \to O\) - \(L \to O\) - \(O \to R\) $\(\text{Ciphertext: } \mathbf{K \ H \ O \ O \ R}\)$

docs.title: 2. Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Cryptography:
docs.text:
• Symmetric-Key Cryptography (e.g., AES, DES): The sender and receiver share the same secret key. Very fast, ideal for encrypting bulk data. Challenge: Secure key exchange.
  • Public-Key Cryptography (e.g., RSA, ECC): Each entity has a mathematically linked key pair:
  • Public Key (\(K_B^+\)): Shared openly with the world.
  • Private Key (\(K_B^-\)): Kept strictly secret by the owner.
  • Confidentiality: Sender encrypts with Bob's Public Key \(K_B^+\). Only Bob's Private Key \(K_B^-\) can decrypt it!

docs.title: 3. Digital Signatures (Providing Integrity & Authenticity):
docs.text:
• To prove identity and guarantee the message was not modified, Alice signs the message hash with her Private Key \(K_A^-\): $\(\text{Signature} = \text{Encrypt}_{K_A^-}(\text{Hash}(M))\)$
  • Anyone can verify the signature using Alice's Public Key \(K_A^+\). Because only Alice knows \(K_A^-\), she cannot deny having sent it (Non-Repudiation).

docs.title: 4.1 Encryption / Decryption Pipeline
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Alice as Sender (Alice)
    actor Eve as Eavesdropper (Eve)
    actor Bob as Receiver (Bob)

    Note over Alice: Plaintext: "HELLO"<br/>Encrypt with Key (+3)
    Alice->>Bob: Transmits Ciphertext: "KHOOR"
    Note over Eve: Intercepts "KHOOR"<br/>Unintelligible! (Confidentiality Protected)
    Note over Bob: Receives "KHOOR"<br/>Decrypt with Key (-3)<br/>Recovers Plaintext: "HELLO"

docs.title: 4.2 Digital Signature Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Sender Side
        M["Message M"] --> H["Hash Function SHA-256"]
        H --> D["Message Digest"]
        D --> Enc["Encrypt with Sender Private Key"]
        Enc --> Sig["Digital Signature"]
    end

    subgraph Transit
        M --> Net["Sent over Network"]
        Sig --> Net
    end

    subgraph Receiver Side
        Net --> M2["Received Message M'"]
        Net --> Sig2["Received Signature"]
        M2 --> H2["Compute Hash SHA-256"]
        H2 --> D1["Digest 1"]
        Sig2 --> Dec["Decrypt with Sender Public Key"]
        Dec --> D2["Digest 2"]
        D1 & D2 --> Comp{"Digest 1 == Digest 2 ?"}
        Comp -- Yes --> Valid["✅ Verified! (Authentic & Untampered)"]
        Comp -- No --> Invalid["❌ Tampered! (Reject Message)"]
    end

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step Signing & Verification Mechanism
docs.text:
1. Hashing: Sender passes message \(M\) through a cryptographic hash function (e.g., SHA-256) to produce a fixed-length digest \(H(M)\).
  2. Signing: Sender encrypts \(H(M)\) using their Private Key \(K_{\text{private}}\) to generate the Digital Signature.
  3. Packaging: Sender transmits both the original message \(M\) and the Digital Signature.
  4. Verification: Receiver decrypts the signature using the sender's Public Key \(K_{\text{public}}\) to recover \(H(M)\). Simultaneously, the receiver independently hashes the received message to produce \(H(M')\).
  5. Comparison: If \(H(M) == H(M')\), the receiver is mathematically certain:
  6. The message was not altered in transit (Integrity).
  7. The message originated from the claimed sender (Authenticity).

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text: • Wax Seal on Royal Letters: In medieval times, kings stamped hot wax with their personal signet ring (Digital Signature). If the seal was unbroken upon arrival, the recipient knew the contents had not been tampered with (Integrity) and that the letter genuinely came from the king (Authenticity). Writing the letter in code ensured that rival spies could not read it (Confidentiality).

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python Cryptography Lab)
docs.text:
import hashlib

def caesar_encrypt(plaintext, shift=3):
    ciphertext = ""
    for char in plaintext:
        if char.isalpha():
            base = ord('A') if char.isupper() else ord('a')
            ciphertext += chr((ord(char) - base + shift) % 26 + base)
        else:
            ciphertext += char
    return ciphertext

def caesar_decrypt(ciphertext, shift=3):
    return caesar_encrypt(ciphertext, -shift)

def compute_sha256(data_str):
    return hashlib.sha256(data_str.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()

# 1. Caesar Cipher Verification
plain = "HELLO"
cipher = caesar_encrypt(plain, shift=3)
decrypted = caesar_decrypt(cipher, shift=3)
print(f"Plaintext: {plain} -> Ciphertext: {cipher} -> Decrypted: {decrypted}")

# 2. Integrity Verification via Hashing
msg_original = "Transfer $1,000 to Bob"
msg_tampered = "Transfer $9,000 to Bob"

hash1 = compute_sha256(msg_original)
hash2 = compute_sha256(msg_tampered)

print(f"\nOriginal Hash : {hash1}")
print(f"Tampered Hash : {hash2}")
print("Integrity Check Passed?", hash1 == hash2)

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Confusing Confidentiality with Integrity: Encrypting a message does NOT guarantee it cannot be tampered with. An attacker could flip random bits in the ciphertext. Without an integrity check (hash / MAC), the receiver would decrypt corrupted garbage! * Encrypting with the Wrong Key for Signatures: - To encrypt for Confidentiality: Use the Receiver's Public Key (anyone can send, only receiver can read). - To create a Digital Signature: Use the Sender's Private Key (only sender can sign, anyone can verify).

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From Midterm 261 Q2(c) & Class Note 1 Page 17)
docs.text:
Question: Explain how the three components of the CIA triad can be achieved in network communications. Provide an example of how symmetric encryption and digital signatures satisfy two of these goals.

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Confidentiality: Achieved using symmetric encryption (e.g., AES) or asymmetric public-key encryption. By transforming plaintext into ciphertext using an encryption key, only parties possessing the corresponding decryption key can read the message. 2. Integrity: Achieved using cryptographic hashing (e.g., SHA-256) combined with digital signatures. If an adversary alters even a single bit of the packet during transit, the receiver's computed hash will not match the decrypted signature digest, immediately alerting the recipient to discard the packet. 3. Availability: Achieved using redundant infrastructure, load balancers, rate limiters, firewalls, and DDoS mitigation scrubbing centers to prevent servers from being overwhelmed.

docs.title: Q1. Which cryptographic tool provides both Integrity and Non-Repudiation?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Symmetric-key AES encryption
  • [ ] B) Caesar substitution cipher
  • [x] C) Digital Signature using Private Key
  • [ ] D) Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC-32) Explanation: A digital signature is created using the sender's private key, meaning only they could have signed it (Non-repudiation), and verifies that the message has not changed (Integrity).

docs.title: Q2. In the Caesar cipher with \(K = 4\), what does the word "NETWORK" encrypt to?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) OGVXPSL
  • [x] B) RIWASVO
  • [ ] C) QHWZRUN
  • [ ] D) SDXBTOV Explanation: N(+4)=R, E(+4)=I, T(+4)=X(W), W(+4)=A, O(+4)=S, R(+4)=V, K(+4)=O \(\implies\) RIWASVO.

docs.title: Q3. Alice sends Bob a message encrypted with Bob's public key. What security property does this provide?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Authentication — proves the message came from Alice
  • [x] B) Confidentiality — only Bob's private key can decrypt it, so only Bob can read it
  • [ ] C) Integrity — the message cannot be modified in transit
  • [ ] D) Non-repudiation — Alice cannot deny sending it Explanation: Encrypting with the recipient's public key provides Confidentiality: only the holder of the matching private key (Bob) can decrypt it. It does NOT prove the message came from Alice (anyone could have used Bob's public key).

docs.title: Q4. Alice sends Bob a message signed with her private key. What security property does this provide?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Confidentiality — the message is encrypted
  • [ ] B) Availability — the message will always reach Bob
  • [x] C) Authentication and Non-repudiation — only Alice's private key could have created this signature, proven by her public key
  • [ ] D) Integrity only — the message hash is verified Explanation: A digital signature created with Alice's private key can be verified by anyone using Alice's public key. This provides Authentication (the message came from Alice) and Non-repudiation (Alice cannot deny signing it). Signing with a private key does NOT encrypt the message for confidentiality.

docs.title: Q5. What is the fundamental difference between symmetric and asymmetric cryptography in terms of key distribution?
docs.text:
• [x] A) Symmetric cryptography requires a shared secret key to be securely exchanged beforehand (key distribution problem); asymmetric cryptography eliminates this by using public/private key pairs
  • [ ] B) Symmetric is always faster but asymmetric is more secure
  • [ ] C) Symmetric uses two keys; asymmetric uses one key
  • [ ] D) There is no practical difference — both face identical key distribution challenges Explanation: The core key distribution problem in symmetric cryptography: how do Alice and Bob securely share the secret key? Asymmetric cryptography solves this — Bob publishes his public key (anyone can have it), and only Bob holds his private key. No prior secure channel is needed for key exchange. In practice, asymmetric crypto (expensive) establishes a session key, then symmetric crypto (fast) encrypts the data.

docs.title: Q6. TLS/HTTPS uses a hybrid cryptographic approach. What is the correct sequence?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Symmetric key exchange → Asymmetric session encryption
  • [x] B) Asymmetric key exchange (RSA/ECDH) to establish a shared session key → Symmetric encryption (AES) for data transfer
  • [ ] C) Only asymmetric encryption throughout the entire session
  • [ ] D) Hash-only approach with no encryption for performance Explanation: TLS uses asymmetric cryptography (RSA, ECDHE) to securely establish a shared session key during the handshake. All subsequent application data is encrypted with fast symmetric AES using that session key. This hybrid approach gets the best of both: security of asymmetric key exchange + speed of symmetric bulk encryption.

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Confidentiality: Eavesdroppers cannot read data \(\to\) Encryption.
  • Integrity: Attackers cannot modify data undetected \(\to\) Hashes / Digital Signatures.
  • Availability: Services remain up and responsive \(\to\) DDoS Mitigation & Firewalls.
  • Public Key Rules:
  • Encrypt with Receiver's Public Key for Confidentiality.
  • Sign with Sender's Private Key for Integrity & Authenticity.

docs.title: 🚨 Chapter 02: Network Attacks and Defense Mechanisms
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: Because early Internet protocols operated on implicit trust without built-in cryptographic authentication, modern networks are constantly vulnerable to malicious actors. Network attacks range from stealthy passive observation to active packet manipulation and massive distributed floods. Securing modern infrastructure requires an in-depth understanding of how attackers execute Packet Sniffing, IP Spoofing, and Denial of Service (DoS/DDoS) attacks, and how perimeter defenses like Firewalls mitigate these threats.

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Categorize network attacks into Passive Attacks (e.g., Sniffing) and Active Attacks (e.g., Spoofing, DoS). * Explain how Packet Sniffing works using Network Interface Cards (NIC) in promiscuous mode. * Trace the mechanics of IP Spoofing and explain why IP's stateless nature facilitates impersonation. * Analyze the anatomy of Denial-of-Service (DoS) and Distributed DoS (DDoS) attacks orchestrated via botnets. * Understand the architecture and filtering rules of Packet-Filtering Firewalls and Stateful Inspection Firewalls.

docs.title: 3.1 Passive vs. Active Attacks
docs.text:
• Passive Attacks: The attacker does not modify data streams or disrupt network operation; they secretly listen to and record transmitted traffic.
  • Primary Example: Packet Sniffing / Wiretapping.
  • Defense: End-to-end encryption (TLS, HTTPS, SSH, IPSec).
  • Active Attacks: The attacker injects false packets, alters data in transit, impersonates legitimate hosts, or disables services.
  • Examples: IP Spoofing, Man-in-the-Middle (MitM), DoS / DDoS.
  • Defense: Cryptographic authentication, firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS/IPS).

docs.title: 1. Packet Sniffing (Eavesdropping):
docs.text:
• Mechanism: In broadcast media (Ethernet hubs, unencrypted WiFi), every frame passes by every connected NIC. Normally, a host's NIC discards frames whose destination MAC does not match its own.
  • In Promiscuous Mode, the NIC passes all incoming frames to the operating system regardless of the destination address.
  • Tools like Wireshark and tcpdump intercept unencrypted credentials, emails, and sensitive data.

docs.title: 2. IP Spoofing (Impersonation):
docs.text:
• Mechanism: The standard IPv4 header contains a 32-bit Source IP Address field. However, standard IP software does not verify whether the sender legitimately owns that IP address!
  • An attacker can craft raw IP packets with a forged source address (e.g., inserting the IP address of an authorized server A) to trick destination B into trusting the payload.

docs.title: 3. Denial of Service (DoS) & Distributed DoS (DDoS):
docs.text:
• DoS: A single attacking machine overwhelms a target server’s processing capacity, memory, or link bandwidth by sending a deluge of bogus requests (e.g., SYN flood, Ping flood).
  • DDoS (Distributed): A single attacker (Botmaster) controls thousands of malware-infected compromised devices (Botnet / Zombies). The attacker commands the entire botnet to simultaneously target a single server from thousands of distinct IP addresses across the globe, rendering IP-based blacklisting virtually impossible.

docs.title: 3.3 Defense: Firewalls
docs.text: A Firewall acts as a perimeter barrier between an untrusted external network (Internet) and a trusted internal private network (LAN): * Packet-Filtering Firewall (Stateless): Inspects individual packets independently at Layer 3 and Layer 4 based on: - Source IP and Destination IP - Source Port and Destination Port - Protocol type (TCP, UDP, ICMP) * Stateful Inspection Firewall: Tracks the state of active TCP connections (e.g., SYN sent, established, closed). Only permits incoming packets that belong to an established session initiated by an internal host.

docs.text:
Host A ─────────────[ Switch / Link ]─────────────> Host B
                           │ (Copies Message M)
                           ▼
                    [ Attacker C ] (Sniffing NIC in Promiscuous Mode)
