docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step Attack Mitigation Workflow
docs.text:
1. At Ingress Router: Deploy Ingress Filtering (BCP 38) to verify that outbound packets leaving a network have source IPs belonging strictly to that network's allocated prefix, stopping spoofing at the boundary.
  2. At Perimeter Firewall: Block all unsolicited inbound connection requests (drop TCP SYN packets targeting internal hosts).
  3. At Server Infrastructure:
  4. Deploy SYN Cookies to defend against TCP SYN flood attacks without exhausting kernel connection tables.
  5. Route traffic through Content Delivery Networks (CDN) and DDoS Scrubbing Centers (e.g., Cloudflare, Akamai) that absorb multi-terabit volumetric floods.

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text: • DDoS Analogy (Flash Mob Blocking a Bank Door): If one troublemaker blocks a bank door (DoS), security guards quickly escort them away. But if a criminal rings up 500 unsuspecting strangers from around the city to all run into the bank lobby at the exact same second asking silly questions (DDoS via Botnet), genuine customers cannot enter, and the bank shuts down.

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python Packet Inspection & Filtering)
docs.text:
class Packet:
    def __init__(self, src_ip, dst_ip, src_port, dst_port, protocol, payload=""):
        self.src_ip = src_ip
        self.dst_ip = dst_ip
        self.src_port = src_port
        self.dst_port = dst_port
        self.protocol = protocol
        self.payload = payload

class StatelessFirewall:
    def __init__(self, default_policy="DROP"):
        self.rules = []
        self.default_policy = default_policy

    def add_rule(self, action, src_ip="*", dst_port="*", protocol="*"):
        self.rules.append({
            'action': action,
            'src_ip': src_ip,
            'dst_port': dst_port,
            'protocol': protocol
        })

    def inspect(self, pkt):
        for rule in self.rules:
            ip_match = (rule['src_ip'] == "*" or rule['src_ip'] == pkt.src_ip)
            port_match = (rule['dst_port'] == "*" or rule['dst_port'] == pkt.dst_port)
            proto_match = (rule['protocol'] == "*" or rule['protocol'] == pkt.protocol)

            if ip_match and port_match and proto_match:
                return rule['action']
        return self.default_policy

# Setup Firewall: Allow Web traffic (Port 80/443), drop others
fw = StatelessFirewall(default_policy="DROP")
fw.add_rule(action="ALLOW", dst_port=80, protocol="TCP")
fw.add_rule(action="ALLOW", dst_port=443, protocol="TCP")

# Test Packets
p_valid = Packet("192.168.1.10", "103.4.5.6", 54321, 80, "TCP")
p_malicious_telnet = Packet("192.168.1.10", "103.4.5.6", 54321, 23, "TCP")

print("Web Packet Status   :", fw.inspect(p_valid))           # ALLOW
print("Telnet Packet Status:", fw.inspect(p_malicious_telnet)) # DROP

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Believing Firewalls Prevent Sniffing: Firewalls guard network perimeters; they CANNOT prevent packet sniffing occurring inside an unencrypted internal LAN! Only transport/application layer encryption (TLS/HTTPS) protects against sniffing. * Assuming All DoS Attacks are Volumetric: Some DoS attacks consume very little bandwidth by exploiting software vulnerabilities (e.g., "Ping of Death", Slowloris HTTP attack, or TCP SYN exhaustion).

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 18 & Midterm 261)
docs.text:
Question: Compare Packet Sniffing and IP Spoofing in terms of attack category (active vs. passive) and the primary cryptographic defenses used to nullify them.

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Packet Sniffing: - Category: Passive Attack (does not modify data; silently intercepts frames). - Primary Defense: End-to-End Encryption (TLS / HTTPS / SSH). Even if an eavesdropper captures frames in promiscuous mode, the content appears as random high-entropy ciphertext. 2. IP Spoofing: - Category: Active Attack (crafts and injects forged packet headers). - Primary Defense: Cryptographic Authentication (Digital Signatures / HMAC) and network-layer Ingress Filtering (RFC 2827 / BCP 38) to discard packets with spoofed source addresses.

docs.title: Q1. When a network adapter is switched into "Promiscuous Mode", what behavior changes?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) It transmits data at double bandwidth.
  • [ ] B) It automatically encrypts all outbound frames.
  • [x] C) It passes all frames seen on the wire to the OS, regardless of destination MAC address.
  • [ ] D) It drops all broadcast frames. Explanation: Promiscuous mode bypasses the hardware MAC address filter, forwarding every observed frame to packet capturing software.

docs.title: Q2. What makes a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack significantly harder to mitigate than a standard DoS attack?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) DDoS attacks use higher encryption keys.
  • [x] B) Traffic originates from thousands of distinct, legitimate-looking global IP addresses in a botnet.
  • [ ] C) DDoS packets do not contain IP headers.
  • [ ] D) Firewalls cannot inspect TCP packets. Explanation: Because requests come from thousands of distributed compromised machines, simple IP-based blacklisting drops traffic from innocent third parties and fails to stop the flood.

docs.title: Q3. What makes a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack significantly harder to defend against compared to a standard DoS attack?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) DDoS uses encrypted traffic that firewalls cannot inspect
  • [ ] B) DDoS attacks only target Layer 7 (Application) so Layer 3 firewalls are ineffective
  • [x] C) DDoS originates from thousands of compromised hosts (botnet) simultaneously, making it impossible to block by simply blacklisting a single source IP
  • [ ] D) DDoS attacks are undetectable until the server crashes Explanation: In a DoS attack, traffic originates from a single source — blocking that IP stops the attack. In a DDoS attack, a botnet of thousands of compromised machines (zombies) floods the target simultaneously from diverse, legitimate-looking IPs distributed globally. Rate limiting and IP blacklisting become ineffective at scale.

docs.title: Q4. How does IP Spoofing enable a Reflective DDoS attack?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) The attacker directly sends traffic to the victim using the victim's own IP
  • [x] B) The attacker sends requests to legitimate servers with the victim's IP as the spoofed source address; the servers send amplified responses to the victim
  • [ ] C) IP Spoofing allows the attacker to intercept and replay packets
  • [ ] D) IP Spoofing is only possible on IPv6 networks, not IPv4 Explanation: In a Reflective DDoS (amplification attack): 1) Attacker sends DNS/NTP requests to open servers with the victim's IP as the spoofed source address. 2) Servers send amplified responses (DNS response is 10-100× larger than request) to the victim's IP. 3) Victim receives massive unsolicited traffic. The attacker's real IP is hidden; legitimate servers act as involuntary amplifiers.

docs.title: Q5. A stateful firewall is superior to a packet filter firewall primarily because:
docs.text:
• [ ] A) It operates faster by processing headers without inspecting the payload
  • [x] B) It tracks the state of active TCP connections and only allows packets that belong to an established, legitimate connection — blocking unsolicited inbound packets
  • [ ] C) It can decrypt TLS-encrypted traffic for deep inspection
  • [ ] D) It operates at Layer 7 (Application layer) while packet filters only work at Layer 4 Explanation: A stateful firewall maintains a connection state table tracking all established TCP connections. An inbound packet is only allowed if it corresponds to a connection that was initiated from inside the network. This blocks port scans and unsolicited SYN packets that a simple packet filter (which only inspects individual packets in isolation) might permit based on port number alone.

docs.title: Q6. What is the difference between a worm and a virus in network security context?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Worms are more dangerous because they encrypt files; viruses only delete files
  • [x] B) A worm self-propagates autonomously across networks without requiring a host file or user interaction; a virus requires attaching to a legitimate executable and needs user action to spread
  • [ ] C) There is no practical difference — the terms are used interchangeably
  • [ ] D) Worms only affect servers; viruses only affect end-user devices Explanation: A virus attaches itself to a legitimate program or file and spreads when the infected file is executed or shared. A worm is self-contained and self-replicating — it autonomously scans for and exploits vulnerabilities on networked hosts without user interaction. The Morris Worm (1988) demonstrated this by scanning for Unix vulnerabilities and self-propagating across ARPANET.

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Sniffing: Passive observation \(\to\) Prevented by TLS / HTTPS Encryption.
  • Spoofing: Forging Source IP \(\to\) Prevented by Ingress Filtering & Cryptographic Signatures.
  • DoS/DDoS: Exhausting resources / bandwidth \(\to\) Mitigated by Firewalls, SYN Cookies, CDNs.
  • Stateless vs. Stateful Firewalls: Stateful firewalls track TCP three-way handshake states, rejecting unsolicited incoming packets.

docs.title: 🌐 Module 03: Application Layer and Protocols
docs.text: Welcome to Module 03: Application Layer and Protocols. Sitting at the pinnacle of the networking protocol stack, the Application Layer is where human interaction, web browsing, email communication, and name resolution come to life. This module explores architectural patterns (Client-Server vs. P2P), the abstraction of Sockets, the timing physics of HTTP 1.0/1.1 and Web Caching, the push/pull dynamics of SMTP and IMAP, and the global distributed hierarchy of the Domain Name System (DNS).

docs.title: 🚪 Chapter 01: Application Architectures, Sockets, and Addressing
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: At the Application Layer, network applications consist of programs running on separate end systems that communicate with each other over the network. Developing a network application requires choosing an architectural model (Client-Server or Peer-to-Peer) and interfacing with the operating system’s transport layer protocols via the Socket API.

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Contrast the Client-Server Architecture with the Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Architecture. * Understand the concept of P2P Self-Scalability. * Define what a Socket is and how it functions as the software interface ("door") between application processes and the transport protocol. * Map process-to-process communication using the (IP Address, Port Number) tuple. * Trace concurrent client connections multiplexed into different service ports on a single host.

docs.title: 3.1 Network Application Architectures
docs.text:
Client-Server Architecture                        Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Architecture
          ┌──────────────┐                                ┌─────────┐
          │ Always-on    │                                │  Peer   │◀────────┐
          │ Server Host  │                                └────┬────┘         │
          │ (Fixed IP)   │                                     │              │
          └───┬───┬───┬──┘                                     ▼              ▼
       ┌──────┘   │   └──────┐                            ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐
       ▼          ▼          ▼                            │  Peer   │───▶│  Peer   │
  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐                        └─────────┘    └─────────┘
  │ Client │ │ Client │ │ Client │                        Arbitrary, dynamically connected
  │  (PC)  │ │ (Phone)│ │(Laptop)│                        peers with changing IP addresses
  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘                        (Self-Scalable!)

docs.title: 1. Client-Server Architecture:
docs.text:
• Server: Always-on host with a permanent, well-known IP address. Handles requests from many client hosts (e.g., Google Web Search, Netflix, Web Servers).
  • Bottleneck: If traffic surges dramatically, the central server or its data center bandwidth can become overwhelmed.
  • Clients: End systems (browsers, mobile apps) that initiate communication. Clients do not communicate directly with one another; they communicate strictly through the central server. Clients often have dynamic IP addresses assigned on boot.

docs.title: 2. Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Architecture:
docs.text:
• No dedicated always-on central server.
  • Arbitrary pairs of connected end systems, called Peers, communicate directly with one another.
  • Self-Scalability: As new peers join the network to download files, they simultaneously upload file chunks to other peers. Each new peer brings new service capacity as well as new service demand!
  • Examples: BitTorrent, Skype (originally), Bitcoin blockchain.

docs.title: 3.2 What is a Socket?
docs.text:
• A process on one host sends messages into, and receives messages from, the network through a software interface called a Socket.
  • The "Door" Analogy: A process is like a house, and its socket is its front door. When a process wants to send a message to another process on another host, it pushes the message out its socket door into the street (transport layer). The underlying network infrastructure carries the message to the destination house's door (destination socket).
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Application Layer (Process: Chrome Browser / Python)  │
│                                                        │
│                  ┌─────────────────┐                   │
│                  │  SOCKET (Door)  │                   │
└──────────────────┴────────┬────────┴───────────────────┘
                            │ API Control Boundary
┌───────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┐
│  Transport Layer Protocol (TCP / UDP)                  │
│  (Managed by Operating System Kernel)                  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 3.3 Addressing Processes: IP + Port
docs.text: An IP address alone is insufficient to send a packet to a program because a single computer runs multiple network programs simultaneously (e.g., Web browser, Spotify, Zoom, Discord). * IP Address (32-bit): Identifies the host computer on the global Internet. (Like the postal address of a multi-story apartment building). * Port Number (16-bit, values 0 to 65535): Identifies the specific receiving application process inside that host computer. (Like the apartment room number!). * Socket Address: The unique combination of (IP Address : Port Number).

    PB -- "FTP Connection: (IP_B:6666 -> IP_C:21)" --> FTP

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step Socket Establishment
docs.text:
1. Server Binds & Listens: The server creates a socket, binds it to a well-known port (e.g., Port 80), and listens for incoming connections.
  2. Client Initiates Connection: The client creates a socket and asks the operating system for a temporary, dynamic ephemeral port (e.g., Port 5555).
  3. Transport Handshake: The client's OS initiates a TCP 3-way handshake targeting (Server_IP : 80).
  4. Accept & Communication: Once connected, both processes read and write byte streams through their respective socket descriptors.

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text:
• Office Building Analogy:
  • To reach the HR Department at Google HQ:
  • 1600 Amphitheatre Pkwy, Mountain View, CA = IP Address (locates the building).
  • Suite #402 (HR Desk) = Port Number (locates the specific department).
  • The mailbox slot on the door of Suite 402 = Socket (the interface through which letters are dropped and retrieved).

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python TCP Socket Client & Server)
Server (server.py):
docs.text:
import socket

server_ip = "127.0.0.1"
server_port = 8080

# 1. Create a TCP socket (AF_INET = IPv4, SOCK_STREAM = TCP)
with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as s:
    s.bind((server_ip, server_port))
    s.listen(5)
    print(f"[*] Server listening on {server_ip}:{server_port}")

    conn, addr = s.accept()
    with conn:
        print(f"[+] Connection accepted from {addr}")
        data = conn.recv(1024)
        print(f"[*] Received message: {data.decode('utf-8')}")
        conn.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n\r\nHello from Python Server!")

docs.title: Client (client.py):
docs.text:
import socket

server_ip = "127.0.0.1"
server_port = 8080

with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as s:
    s.connect((server_ip, server_port))
    s.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n\r\n")
    response = s.recv(1024)
    print("[*] Server Response:\n", response.decode('utf-8'))

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Assuming Port Numbers Must Match: A client connecting from Port 5555 to a server's Port 80 is completely normal. The source port and destination port are independent 16-bit integers! * Confusing Sockets with Ports: A port is a 16-bit number; a socket is the software endpoint object instantiated by the OS that binds a process to a specific port and IP.

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 21: Midterm 252 Q2(b))
docs.text:
Question: Host A has IP address IP_A and runs a web browser using port 5555. Host B has IP address IP_B and runs an FTP client using port 6666. Both connect simultaneously to Server C with IP address IP_C, which runs a Web service (port 80) and an FTP service (port 21). 1. Specify the source and destination socket addresses (IP, Port) for the connection from Host A to Server C. 2. Specify the source and destination socket addresses for the connection from Host B to Server C. 3. How does Server C differentiate between the incoming packets?

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Connection 1 (Host A \(\to\) Server C Web Service): - Source Socket: (IP_A : 5555) - Destination Socket: (IP_C : 80) 2. Connection 2 (Host B \(\to\) Server C FTP Service): - Source Socket: (IP_B : 6666) - Destination Socket: (IP_C : 21) 3. Differentiation at Server C: - Server C’s transport layer inspects the destination port in the TCP header: - Packets arriving with destination port 80 are directed to the HTTP daemon process socket. - Packets arriving with destination port 21 are directed to the FTP daemon process socket.

docs.title: Q1. Which statement best describes the self-scalability property of P2P architectures?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) P2P networks require more expensive routers.
  • [x] B) Peers add service capacity by uploading chunks at the same time they create demand by downloading.
  • [ ] C) P2P does not require TCP/IP protocol support.
  • [ ] D) P2P servers have static IP addresses. Explanation: In P2P, every consumer is also a producer, meaning system capacity scales naturally with the user base.

docs.title: Q2. What is the standard well-known port number for secure HTTPS web traffic?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) 21
  • [ ] B) 25
  • [ ] C) 80
  • [x] D) 443 Explanation: Standard HTTP uses port 80; TLS-encrypted HTTPS uses port 443.

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Client-Server: Centralized, always-on server, clients initiate communication.
  • Peer-to-Peer: Distributed, self-scaling, no central server required.
  • Socket: Software interface door connecting application processes to OS transport protocols.
  • Addressing: (IP : Port) uniquely identifies an application process endpoint on the Internet.

docs.title: 🌐 Chapter 02: HTTP and Web Caching Mechanics
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: The HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is the network backbone of the World Wide Web. Operating over TCP (port 80 for HTTP, port 443 for HTTPS), HTTP defines how Web clients request Web pages and how Web servers transfer them. A deep understanding of HTTP requires analyzing the performance impact of Non-Persistent vs. Persistent Connections, session management via Cookies, and network bandwidth conservation via Web Caching (Proxy Servers).

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Explain why HTTP is fundamentally a stateless protocol and how Cookies maintain state across transactions. * Contrast the performance of Non-Persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.0) with Persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.1). * Calculate exact web page download times involving base HTML and multiple embedded objects (CSS, images). * Analyze how Web Caching / Forward Proxies reduce access link utilization, propagation delay, and server load. * Understand the Conditional GET header (If-Modified-Since) and the 304 Not Modified response code.

docs.title: 3.1 HTTP Overview & Characteristics
docs.text:
• Port: 80 (standard HTTP) over reliable TCP.
  • Client-Server Model: Web browser (Client) issues HTTP Request; Web server replies with HTTP Response.
  • Statelessness: An HTTP server maintains no information about past client requests. If a client requests the same web page twice in two seconds, the server treats the second request completely independently.
  • Cookies (Making HTTP Stateful): To support shopping carts, logins, and personalization, HTTP uses cookies:
  • Server sends Set-cookie: 1678 in HTTP response header.
  • Client browser stores the cookie on disk.
  • In subsequent requests to that domain, client sends Cookie: 1678 in the request header.

docs.title: 1. Non-Persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.0):
docs.text:
• A brand-new TCP connection is opened and closed for each and every individual web object (HTML file, CSS, JavaScript, image).
  • For each object:
  • \(1\text{ RTT}\) to establish the TCP 3-way handshake.
  • \(1\text{ RTT}\) to send the HTTP request and receive the first bytes of the response.
  • \(\text{FTT}\) (File Transmission Time) to transmit the file bytes.
  • Total Time per Object: $\(\text{Time}_{\text{object}} = 2\text{RTT} + \text{FTT}\)$
  • Total Download Time for \(N\) objects (Sequential): $\(\text{Total Time}_{\text{Non-Persistent}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (2\text{RTT}_i + \text{FTT}_i)\)$

docs.title: 2. Persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.1):
docs.text:
• The server leaves the TCP connection open after sending a response. Subsequent requests and responses between the same client and server are sent over the same existing connection.
  • The initial connection setup takes \(1\text{ RTT}\). Each subsequent object requires only \(1\text{ RTT} + \text{FTT}\)!
  • Total Download Time for \(N\) objects (Persistent without pipelining): $\(\text{Total Time}_{\text{Persistent}} = 1\text{RTT}_{\text{connection}} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} (1\text{RTT}_i + \text{FTT}_i)\)$
  • File Transmission Time (FTT) Formula: $\(\text{FTT} = \frac{\text{Object Size (bits)}}{\text{Bandwidth (bps)}} = \frac{\text{Object Size (Bytes)} \times 8}{\text{Link Speed (bps)}}\)$

docs.title: 3.3 Web Caching (Proxy Servers)
docs.text: A Web Cache (Proxy Server) is a network entity that satisfies HTTP requests on behalf of an origin Web server: 1. Browser is configured to send all HTTP requests to the local proxy cache. 2. If the requested object is in the cache (Cache Hit): The proxy immediately returns the object to the client. (Extremely low latency!). 3. If not in the cache (Cache Miss): The proxy opens a connection to the origin server, retrieves the object, saves a local copy, and delivers it to the client.

docs.title: Conditional GET (If-Modified-Since):
docs.text:
To prevent serving stale cached content, the proxy issues an HTTP GET with the header: 

If-Modified-Since: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT
* If unchanged: Origin server responds with HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified (no message body!). Saves bandwidth! * If modified: Origin server responds with HTTP/1.1 200 OK and sends the updated file body.

docs.title: 4.1 Non-Persistent vs. Persistent HTTP Timing Ladder (From CN Class Note 1, Page 22)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client
    actor Server

    Note over Client,Server: Non-Persistent HTTP (Repeats for EVERY object)
    Client->>Server: TCP SYN (Connection Request)
    Server-->>Client: TCP SYN-ACK (Connection Response) -- [1 RTT]
    Client->>Server: HTTP GET Request
    Server-->>Client: HTTP Response + Data Body -- [1 RTT + FTT]

    Note over Client,Server: Persistent HTTP (Single TCP Setup)
    Client->>Server: TCP SYN
    Server-->>Client: TCP SYN-ACK -- [1 RTT Connection Setup]
    Client->>Server: HTTP GET (HTML)
    Server-->>Client: HTTP Response (HTML) -- [1 RTT + FTT]
    Client->>Server: HTTP GET (Image 1)
    Server-->>Client: HTTP Response (Image 1) -- [1 RTT + FTT]
    Note over Client,Server: Connection remains open for all objects!

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step Retrieval Walkthrough
docs.text: Tracing a web page consisting of index.html referencing 2 CSS files and 8 Images: 1. Under Non-Persistent HTTP: - 1 TCP connection for index.html (\(2\text{RTT} + \text{FTT}_{\text{html}}\)). - 2 sequential TCP connections for CSS (\(2 \times (2\text{RTT} + \text{FTT}_{\text{css}})\)). - 8 sequential TCP connections for Images (\(8 \times (2\text{RTT} + \text{FTT}_{\text{img}})\)). - Total = 11 separate TCP handshakes and teardowns! 2. Under Persistent HTTP: - Single TCP connection created (\(1\text{ RTT}\)). - index.html fetched (\(1\text{ RTT} + \text{FTT}_{\text{html}}\)). - Both CSS fetched over same connection (\(2 \times (1\text{ RTT} + \text{FTT}_{\text{css}})\)). - All 8 images fetched over same connection (\(8 \times (1\text{ RTT} + \text{FTT}_{\text{img}})\)). - Massive time savings!

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text:
• Grocery Store Trip Analogy:
  • Non-Persistent HTTP: You go to the supermarket, drive through the parking gate, enter the store, buy one apple, drive home, and park. Then you realize you need milk, drive all the way back, pay the gate, buy milk, and drive home.
  • Persistent HTTP: You drive to the supermarket once, enter the store, and buy the apple, milk, bread, and eggs in one single visit before driving home.

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python HTTP Download Time Calculator)
docs.text:
def calculate_http_time(rtt_s, objects, link_bandwidth_bps, persistent=False):
    """
    objects: list of dicts with {'name': str, 'size_bytes': int, 'count': int}
    """
    total_time = 0.0

    if persistent:
        # 1 RTT initial connection setup
        total_time += rtt_s

        for obj in objects:
            ftt = (obj['size_bytes'] * 8) / link_bandwidth_bps
            time_per_item = rtt_s + ftt
            total_time += obj['count'] * time_per_item
    else:
        for obj in objects:
            ftt = (obj['size_bytes'] * 8) / link_bandwidth_bps
            time_per_item = 2 * rtt_s + ftt
            total_time += obj['count'] * time_per_item

    return total_time * 1000 # Return in milliseconds

# Test Case matching Midterm 261 Q2(b) & Class Note 1, Page 7 & 23:
# RTT = 0.2 ms = 0.0002 s, Bandwidth = 1 Gbps = 1e9 bps
# HTML: 100 KB = 100 * 10^3 Bytes
# CSS : 2 files, 150 KB each
# Image: 8 files, 2 MB each = 2 * 10^6 Bytes
web_objects = [
    {'name': 'HTML',  'size_bytes': 100e3, 'count': 1},
    {'name': 'CSS',   'size_bytes': 150e3, 'count': 2},
    {'name': 'Image', 'size_bytes': 2e6,   'count': 8}
]

t_non_persistent = calculate_http_time(0.0002, web_objects, 1e9, persistent=False)
t_persistent     = calculate_http_time(0.0002, web_objects, 1e9, persistent=True)

print(f"Non-Persistent Total Time: {t_non_persistent:.2f} ms")
print(f"Persistent Total Time    : {t_persistent:.2f} ms")

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Forgetting the Initial TCP RTT in Persistent HTTP: Remember the \(+1\text{ RTT}\) at the beginning for the connection setup! * Unit Conversion Errors: When computing \(\text{FTT} = \frac{\text{Bytes} \times 8}{\text{bps}}\), ensure that \(1\text{ Gbps} = 10^9\text{ bps}\), \(1\text{ MB} = 10^6\text{ Bytes}\), and \(\text{RTT} = 0.2\text{ ms} = 0.0002\text{ seconds}\).

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 7 & 23: Midterm 261 Q2(b))
docs.text:
Question: A client is downloading a web page consisting of: * \(1\text{ base HTML file}\) of size \(100\text{ KB}\) (\(100 \times 10^3\text{ Bytes}\)). * \(2\text{ CSS files}\) of size \(150\text{ KB}\) each (\(150 \times 10^3\text{ Bytes}\)). * \(8\text{ Image files}\) of size \(2\text{ MB}\) each (\(2 \times 10^6\text{ Bytes}\)). Given link bandwidth \(R = 1\text{ Gbps} = 10^9\text{ bps}\) and \(\text{RTT} = 0.2\text{ ms}\). Calculate total retrieval time for: 1. Non-persistent HTTP 2. Persistent HTTP (without pipelining)

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Calculate FTT for each object type: * \(\text{FTT}_{\text{HTML}} = \frac{100 \times 10^3 \times 8}{10^9} = \frac{800,000}{10^9} = 0.0008\text{ s} = \mathbf{0.8\text{ ms}}\) * \(\text{FTT}_{\text{CSS}} = \frac{150 \times 10^3 \times 8}{10^9} = \frac{1,200,000}{10^9} = 0.0012\text{ s} = \mathbf{1.2\text{ ms}}\) * \(\text{FTT}_{\text{Image}} = \frac{2 \times 10^6 \times 8}{10^9} = \frac{16,000,000}{10^9} = 0.016\text{ s} = \mathbf{16.0\text{ ms}}\)

  1. Case 1: Non-Persistent HTTP (\(2\text{RTT} + \text{FTT}\) per object):
  2. HTML: \((2 \times 0.2) + 0.8 = 0.4 + 0.8 = 1.2\text{ ms}\)
  3. 2 CSS: \(2 \times [(2 \times 0.2) + 1.2] = 2 \times [0.4 + 1.2] = 2 \times 1.6 = 3.2\text{ ms}\)

  4. 8 Images: \(8 \times [(2 \times 0.2) + 16] = 8 \times [0.4 + 16] = 8 \times 16.4 = 131.2\text{ ms}\) $\(\text{Total Time} = 1.2 + 3.2 + 131.2 = \mathbf{135.6\text{ ms}}\)$

  5. Case 2: Persistent HTTP (\(1\text{RTT}_{\text{conn}} + \sum(1\text{RTT} + \text{FTT})\)):

  6. TCP Connection Setup: \(1\text{ RTT} = 0.2\text{ ms}\)
  7. HTML: \(0.2 + 0.8 = 1.0\text{ ms}\)
  8. 2 CSS: \(2 \times (0.2 + 1.2) = 2 \times 1.4 = 2.8\text{ ms}\)
  9. 8 Images: \(8 \times (0.2 + 16) = 8 \times 16.2 = 129.6\text{ ms}\) $\(\text{Total Time} = 0.2 + 1.0 + 2.8 + 129.6 = \mathbf{133.6\text{ ms}}\)$

docs.title: Q1. What HTTP status code is returned when a cached object on a proxy is still fresh and unmodified?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) 200 OK
  • [ ] B) 404 Not Found
  • [x] C) 304 Not Modified
  • [ ] D) 301 Moved Permanently Explanation: A conditional GET using If-Modified-Since receives a 304 Not Modified response with an empty body, saving bandwidth.

docs.title: Q2. Why is HTTP called a "Stateless" protocol?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) It cannot transmit multimedia objects.
  • [x] B) The server preserves no state or history about past client requests.
  • [ ] C) It operates exclusively over UDP.
  • [ ] D) It does not require an IP address. Explanation: HTTP servers process each request independently without retaining memory of previous transactions from the same client.

docs.title: Q3. A web page contains 1 base HTML file and 8 embedded objects. With non-persistent HTTP (no parallel connections) and RTT = 100 ms, file transmission time is negligible. What is the total retrieval time?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) \(200\ \text{ms}\) (1 RTT for base + 1 RTT shared for all objects)
  • [ ] B) \(900\ \text{ms}\) (9 × RTT)
  • [x] C) \(1800\ \text{ms}\) (9 objects × 2 RTT each = 18 RTT × 100 ms)
  • [ ] D) \(1000\ \text{ms}\) (1 RTT for TCP setup + 9 RTT for objects) Explanation: Non-persistent HTTP: each object requires 2 RTT (1 RTT for TCP handshake + 1 RTT for HTTP GET/response). Total = 9 objects × 2 RTT = 18 RTT = 18 × 100 ms = 1800 ms.

docs.title: Q4. What is the purpose of the HTTP If-Modified-Since header in conditional GET requests?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) To specify how long the browser should cache the object
  • [ ] B) To request a specific version of an object by its hash
  • [x] C) To allow the browser/proxy cache to validate its cached copy without re-downloading the full object — server replies 304 Not Modified if unchanged
  • [ ] D) To tell the server to send the response before the client's connection is established Explanation: The conditional GET mechanism: the browser sends If-Modified-Since: <date of cached copy>. If the object hasn't changed, the server returns HTTP 304 Not Modified (no body) — saving bandwidth. If changed, server returns HTTP 200 OK with the full new object. This is the core cache validation mechanism.

docs.title: Q5. What is the fundamental difference between HTTP/1.1 persistent connections with pipelining versus without pipelining?
docs.text:
• [x] A) Without pipelining: client waits for each response before sending the next request (sequential). With pipelining: client sends multiple requests without waiting, dramatically reducing total retrieval time
  • [ ] B) Pipelining opens multiple TCP connections simultaneously
  • [ ] C) Pipelining only works with encrypted HTTPS connections
  • [ ] D) Without pipelining uses UDP; with pipelining uses TCP Explanation: Without pipelining: Request 1 → Response 1 → Request 2 → Response 2 (each transaction sequential). With pipelining: Request 1, Request 2, Request 3 sent back-to-back without waiting → Response 1, Response 2, Response 3. Total retrieval time ≈ 1 RTT for all pipelined requests (versus N RTTs without pipelining). HTTP/2 extended this further with multiplexing.

docs.title: Q6. How does a Web Cache (proxy server) reduce both end-user delay AND origin server load simultaneously?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) It compresses responses to reduce file sizes
  • [ ] B) It pre-fetches content before users request it
  • [x] C) By serving locally cached copies to clients without contacting the origin server — the client experiences LAN-speed delivery, and the origin server receives fewer requests
  • [ ] D) It performs DNS resolution locally to speed up name lookups Explanation: When a request is a cache hit, the web proxy serves the cached copy immediately at LAN speed (much faster than WAN RTT to origin). When a cache miss occurs, the proxy fetches from the origin, caches it, and serves it. Net effect: clients get faster responses; the institutional link to the Internet is less congested; origin servers handle fewer requests.

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Non-Persistent HTTP: \(n \times (2\text{RTT} + \text{FTT})\)
  • Persistent HTTP: \(\text{RTT}_{\text{conn}} + \sum (1\text{RTT} + \text{FTT})\)
  • Cookies: Enable stateful sessions (e.g., shopping carts) over stateless HTTP via Set-Cookie and Cookie headers.
  • Web Caches: Proxies sit between clients and origin servers, reducing latency and saving access link bandwidth.

docs.title: ✉️ Chapter 03: Electronic Mail Architecture and SMTP
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: Electronic mail is one of the earliest and most fundamental distributed applications on the Internet. Unlike the Web (which is predominantly a client-driven pull architecture), email operates as a multi-stage store-and-forward push architecture. Understanding email requires dissecting the interaction between User Agents (UAs), Mail Servers, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), and mail access retrieval protocols (POP3, IMAP, and HTTP).

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Identify the key architectural components of the email system: User Agents (MUA), Mail Servers (MTA), Mailboxes, and Outgoing Message Queues. * Explain the role and mechanics of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) over TCP port 25. * Contrast SMTP (Push Protocol) with HTTP (Pull Protocol). * Trace the protocols used at each hop when an email is sent from a web-based client (e.g., Gmail) to a destination mail server and retrieved by a recipient. * Differentiate between POP3 (download-and-delete) and IMAP (server-synchronized folder hierarchy).

docs.title: 3.1 Email System Architecture
docs.text:
┌─────────────┐      HTTP / SMTP      ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ User Agent  │ ────────────────────> │  Sender's Mail Server   │
│ (Ashiq PC)  │                       │  (e.g., smtp.gmail.com) │
└─────────────┘                       │ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
                                      │ │ Mailbox │ │ Message │ │
                                      │ │         │ │  Queue  │ │
                                      │ └─────────┘ └────┬────┘ │
                                      └──────────────────┼──────┘
                                                         │
                                                         │ SMTP (Push)
                                                         │ Port 25
                                                         ▼
┌─────────────┐      POP3 / IMAP /    ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ User Agent  │ <──────────────────── │ Receiver's Mail Server  │
│  (Riad PC)  │          HTTP         │  (e.g., mail.yahoo.com) │
└─────────────┘                       │ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
                                      │ │ Mailbox │ │ Message │ │
                                      │ │         │ │  Queue  │ │
                                      │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ │
                                      └─────────────────────────┘
  1. User Agent (Mail Reader): Software that allows users to compose, send, and read messages (e.g., Outlook, Apple Mail, Webmail like Gmail web interface).
  2. Mail Server (Core Infrastructure):
  3. Mailbox: Stores incoming messages destined for local users on that domain.
  4. Message Queue: Holds outgoing messages waiting to be transmitted to remote mail servers.
  5. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol):
  6. Used to transfer mail from the sender's mail server to the recipient's mail server.
  7. Runs over TCP (Port 25).
  8. A strictly Push Protocol: The sending server initiates the connection and pushes the message to the receiving server.
  9. Legacy constraint: Originally restricted message bodies to 7-bit ASCII. Multimedia attachments are encoded into ASCII via MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions).

docs.title: 3.2 HTTP vs. SMTP Comparison
docs.text: Feature HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) Primary Direction Pull Protocol: Client pulls data from the server on demand. Push Protocol: Sending mail server pushes data to the receiving server. Port & Transport Port 80 (HTTP) / 443 (HTTPS) over TCP Port 25 (Server-to-Server SMTP) over TCP Data Encoding Encapsulates binary data natively (images, video, audio) in response body. Originally restricted to 7-bit ASCII; binary requires MIME encoding. Object Handling Each object is encapsulated in its own HTTP response message. All objects (body text + attachments) are packaged into a single multipart message.

docs.title: 3.3 Mail Access Protocols: Retrieving Email from Mailboxes
docs.text: SMTP is designed strictly as a push protocol; it cannot be used by a recipient to pull emails from their mailbox because the recipient's machine is typically not an always-on server with a public IP address! Special retrieval protocols are required: 1. POP3 (Post Office Protocol Version 3 - Port 110): - Simple download-and-delete model. Downloads emails to the local client and removes them from the server. - Limitation: Cannot synchronize read/unread states or folders across multiple devices (phone vs laptop). 2. IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol - Port 143): - Advanced server-synchronized model. Keeps all messages permanently on the server. - Allows users to organize messages into folders, search remotely, and sync state across all devices. 3. HTTP / Webmail: - User interacts with their mailbox via a web browser using standard HTTPS.

docs.title: 4.1 End-to-End Email Transmission Flow (From CN Class Note 1, Page 25)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Sender as Sender (Ashiq)
    participant SendMTA as Sender Mail Server (Gmail)
    participant RecvMTA as Recipient Mail Server (Yahoo)
    actor Receiver as Recipient (Riad)

    Note over Sender,SendMTA: Step 1: Upload Message to Sender Server
    Sender->>SendMTA: HTTP POST / SMTP (Message placed in Outgoing Queue)

    Note over SendMTA,RecvMTA: Step 2: Server-to-Server Relay via SMTP
    SendMTA->>RecvMTA: TCP SYN (Port 25)
    RecvMTA-->>SendMTA: TCP SYN-ACK
    SendMTA->>RecvMTA: HELO / MAIL FROM / RCPT TO / DATA (Message Body)
    RecvMTA-->>SendMTA: 250 Message accepted for delivery
    Note over RecvMTA: Placed into Riad's Mailbox!

    Note over RecvMTA,Receiver: Step 3: Message Retrieval
    Receiver->>RecvMTA: IMAP / POP3 / HTTPS Connection
    RecvMTA-->>Receiver: Delivers email message to Riad's screen

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step SMTP Dialogue Example
docs.text:
A direct SMTP exchange between mail servers over TCP: 

S: 220 mail.yahoo.com Simple Mail Transfer Service Ready
C: HELO mail.gmail.com
S: 250 Hello mail.gmail.com
C: MAIL FROM: <ashiq@gmail.com>
S: 250 2.1.0 Sender OK
C: RCPT TO: <riad@yahoo.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Recipient OK
C: DATA
S: 354 Start mail input; end with <CRLF>.<CRLF>
C: Subject: Computer Networks Exam Notes
C: Hi Riad, here are the solved class notes.
C: .
S: 250 2.0.0 OK: message queued 12345
C: QUIT
S: 221 Closing transmission channel

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text:
• Physical Post Office Relay:
  • You write a letter and drop it in the local blue collection box (HTTP/SMTP to Sender Server).
  • The local post office truck transports and delivers the letter bags to the destination city sorting hub (SMTP Server-to-Server transfer).
  • The destination post office puts the letter in the recipient’s physical P.O. Box (Mailbox).
  • The recipient drives to the post office with their key to unlock their box and pick up the letter (IMAP/POP3 retrieval).

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python SMTP Sending Simulation)
docs.text:
import smtplib
from email.mime.text import MIMEText
from email.mime.multipart import MIMEMultipart

def simulate_email_send(sender, receiver, subject, body):
    # Construct MIME multipart message
    msg = MIMEMultipart()
    msg['From'] = sender
    msg['To'] = receiver
    msg['Subject'] = subject
    msg.attach(MIMEText(body, 'plain'))

    print("[*] Email Message Constructed:")
    print(f"    From   : {msg['From']}")
    print(f"    To     : {msg['To']}")
    print(f"    Subject: {msg['Subject']}")
    print("    Payload:\n", msg.as_string())

    # Simulated SMTP interaction:
    print("[+] Connecting to SMTP server over TCP port 25...")
    print(f"[+] Handshaking: MAIL FROM:<{sender}> -> RCPT TO:<{receiver}>")
    print("[+] Status 250: Message accepted for delivery!")

simulate_email_send(
    sender="ashiq@gmail.com",
    receiver="riad@yahoo.com",
    subject="CSE3711 Class Notes",
    body="Hey! All diagrams and formulas are analyzed."
)

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Assuming SMTP is Used to Read Mail: SMTP is strictly a Push Protocol used to send mail. It CANNOT be used by an end-user to read or download mail from a server mailbox! That requires POP3, IMAP, or HTTP. * Confusing Mailbox with Message Queue: The Mailbox stores incoming mail waiting for the local user to read; the Message Queue holds outgoing mail waiting to be sent to remote servers.

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 8 & 27: Midterm Exam Scenario)
docs.text:
Question: Rahman sends an email from his web-based Gmail account on his laptop to his friend Karim, who uses a Mozilla Thunderbird desktop mail client to read his Yahoo email. 1. Identify the application-layer protocols used across each hop of the communication. 2. Explain two key differences between HTTP and SMTP.

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Hop-by-Hop Protocols: * Hop 1 (Rahman's Laptop \(\to\) Gmail Mail Server): HTTP / HTTPS. Since Rahman uses a web-based client in a browser, he communicates with the Gmail web server over HTTP. * Hop 2 (Gmail Mail Server \(\to\) Yahoo Mail Server): SMTP (over TCP Port 25). Server-to-server mail relay is universally handled by SMTP. * Hop 3 (Yahoo Mail Server \(\to\) Karim's Thunderbird Client): IMAP (or POP3). Because Karim uses a desktop email client, he pulls his messages from the Yahoo mailbox using IMAP. 2. Two Key Differences: * Pull vs. Push: HTTP is primarily a pull protocol where clients request data from a server; SMTP is a push protocol where the sending server pushes data to the receiving server. * Data Handling: HTTP allows arbitrary binary data in the response body; SMTP was originally designed for 7-bit ASCII text and requires MIME encoding for binary attachments.

docs.title: Q1. Which protocol is used by an intermediate mail server to forward an email to the recipient's mail server?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) POP3
  • [ ] B) IMAP
  • [x] C) SMTP
  • [ ] D) HTTP Explanation: Server-to-server email forwarding across the Internet is performed exclusively by SMTP over TCP port 25.

docs.title: Q2. Why is IMAP generally preferred over POP3 on modern devices?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) IMAP uses less bandwidth than POP3.
  • [ ] B) IMAP encrypts emails automatically while POP3 cannot.
  • [x] C) IMAP keeps emails synchronized on the server across multiple devices (phone, laptop).
  • [ ] D) IMAP operates over UDP. Explanation: IMAP maintains the folder hierarchy and message read/unread status on the central server, allowing seamless multi-device synchronization.

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• SMTP (Port 25): Push protocol used by clients to send mail and by mail servers to relay mail to other servers.
  • POP3 (Port 110): Download-and-delete retrieval protocol.
  • IMAP (Port 143): Server-synchronized retrieval protocol.
  • Webmail: Uses HTTP/HTTPS between browser and local mail server, but underlying server-to-server transfer remains standard SMTP!

docs.title: 1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: Humans prefer mnemonic, readable hostnames like www.google.com or ucam.uiu.ac.bd, whereas routers and packet switches navigate using fixed-length numerical IP addresses like 142.251.211.78. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the Internet’s global, distributed directory service that translates human-friendly hostnames into machine-routable IP addresses. Running at the Application Layer over UDP (Port 53), DNS is a masterclass in hierarchical database design, distributed scalability, and caching.

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Explain why DNS is implemented as a distributed, hierarchical database rather than a single centralized server. * Navigate the DNS hierarchy: Root DNS Servers, Top-Level Domain (TLD) Servers, and Authoritative DNS Servers. * Trace the complete 8-step resolution sequence of an Iterative DNS Query versus a Recursive DNS Query. * Understand why recursive queries create severe vulnerabilities and excessive load on Root DNS servers. * Construct and interpret the four fundamental DNS Resource Records (RR): Type A, Type NS, Type CNAME, and Type MX. * Analyze how Local DNS Caching eliminates repetitive global query overhead.

docs.title: 3.1 Why a Distributed Database?
docs.text: A centralized DNS server with a single giant database of all mappings would fail catastrophically due to: * Single Point of Failure: If the central server crashes, the entire global Internet goes offline. * Traffic Volume: Trillions of queries per day would overwhelm any single data center. * Distant Centralized Database: Queries from Bangladesh to a server in California would suffer huge propagation delays. * Maintenance Nightmare: Millions of domain records update every day.

docs.title: 3.2 The DNS Hierarchy
docs.text:
┌─────────────┐
                               │  Root DNS   │
                               │   Servers   │
                               └──────┬──────┘
             ┌────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
             ▼                        ▼                        ▼
       ┌───────────┐            ┌───────────┐            ┌───────────┐
       │ .com TLD  │            │ .edu TLD  │            │  .bd TLD  │
       └─────┬─────┘            └─────┬─────┘            └─────┬─────┘
             │                        │                        │
             ▼                        ▼                        ▼
     ┌───────────────┐        ┌───────────────┐        ┌───────────────┐
     │  google.com   │        │   nyu.edu     │        │   uiu.ac.bd   │
     │ Authoritative │        │ Authoritative │        │ Authoritative │
     └───────────────┘        └───────────────┘        └───────────────┘
  1. Root DNS Servers: Over 1,000 replicated instances worldwide organized under 13 logical root authorities (managed by ICANN). Returns referrals to appropriate TLD servers.
  2. Top-Level Domain (TLD) Servers: Responsible for generic top-level domains (.com, .org, .net, .edu) and country-code top-level domains (.bd, .uk, .jp).
  3. Authoritative DNS Servers: Owned and maintained by organizations or service providers. Holds the actual definitive mappings for public hosts (e.g., UIU’s server holds mappings for ucam.uiu.ac.bd).
  4. Local DNS Server (Default Name Server): Each ISP, university, or home router has a local DNS server (e.g., 8.8.8.8 Google DNS, 1.1.1.1 Cloudflare). The local DNS server acts as the client’s proxy, executing the resolution on its behalf.

docs.title: 1. Iterative Query (Standard Industry Practice):
docs.text:
• The queried server replies with the address of the next server to consult rather than finding the answer itself:
  • "I don't know the IP, but ask this TLD server!"
  • The Local DNS server does all the legwork, traveling from Root \(\to\) TLD \(\to\) Authoritative.

docs.title: 2. Recursive Query:
docs.text:
• The contacted server assumes the burden of fully resolving the name itself, recursing up and down the chain and returning the final answer to the client.
  • Why Recursive Queries are Discouraged at Root/TLD:
  • Puts an excessive processing load on Root servers.
  • Leaves root servers highly vulnerable to denial-of-service and cache-poisoning attacks.

docs.title: 3.4 DNS Resource Records (RR)
docs.text:
DNS servers store mappings in 4-tuple Resource Records: $\(\mathbf{(Name, \ Value, \ Type, \ TTL)}\)$

Type Meaning Format of Name and Value Example Record A Hostname to IPv4 Address Name = HostnameValue = IPv4 Address (www.google.com, 142.251.211.78, A, IN) NS Authoritative Name Server for Domain Name = DomainValue = Hostname of Name Server (uiu.ac.bd, ns1.uiu.ac.bd, NS, IN) CNAME Canonical (True) Name for an Alias Name = Alias (Nickname)Value = Canonical Hostname (sch.goo.gl, scholar.google.com, CNAME, IN) MX Mail Server for Domain Name = Mail DomainValue = Hostname of Mail Server (gmail.com, alt1.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com, MX, IN)

docs.title: 4.1 The 8-Step Iterative Query Ladder (From CN Class Note 1, Page 27)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Requesting Host (engineering.nyu.edu)
    participant Local as Local DNS Server (dns.nyu.edu)
    participant Root as Root DNS Server
    participant TLD as .edu TLD DNS Server
    participant Auth as Authoritative DNS (dns.cs.umass.edu)

    Client->>Local: 1. Query: IP for gaia.cs.umass.edu?
    Local->>Root: 2. Query gaia.cs.umass.edu
    Root-->>Local: 3. Referral: Ask .edu TLD server (IP: TLD_IP)
    Local->>TLD: 4. Query gaia.cs.umass.edu
    TLD-->>Local: 5. Referral: Ask Authoritative server (IP: Auth_IP)
    Local->>Auth: 6. Query gaia.cs.umass.edu
    Auth-->>Local: 7. Answer: IP is 128.119.245.12
    Local-->>Client: 8. Delivers final IP 128.119.245.12!

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step Resolution Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Host initiates lookup: User types www.cisco.com into Safari. The OS checks local cache; on a miss, sends a query to the Local DNS server (dns.uiu.ac.bd).
  2. Local to Root: Local DNS queries a Root DNS server.
  3. Root referral: Root returns an NS record pointing to .com TLD servers.
  4. Local to TLD: Local DNS queries the .com TLD server.
  5. TLD referral: TLD returns an NS record pointing to Cisco's authoritative server (ns1.cisco.com).
  6. Local to Authoritative: Local DNS queries ns1.cisco.com.
  7. Authoritative response: Authoritative server returns a Type A record: (www.cisco.com, 72.163.4.161).
  8. Caching & Delivery: Local DNS caches the mapping for the duration of its TTL (Time to Live) and delivers the IP to Safari.

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text:
• Global Telephone Directory Assistance:
  • You want the private phone number of Dr. John at Stanford Hospital.
  • You call the national operator (Root). The operator doesn't have local doctor numbers, but gives you the phone number for California Medical Board (TLD).
  • You call California Medical Board. They give you the switchboard number for Stanford Hospital (Authoritative).
  • You call Stanford Hospital switchboard. They look up their internal directory and give you Dr. John's direct extension (Final IP).

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python DNS Resolver)
docs.text:
import socket

def resolve_hostname(hostname):
    try:
        ip_address = socket.gethostbyname(hostname)
        canonical_name, aliases, ip_list = socket.gethostbyname_ex(hostname)
        return {
            'query_host': hostname,
            'canonical_name': canonical_name,
            'aliases': aliases,
            'ip_addresses': ip_list
        }
    except socket.gaierror as e:
        return {'error': str(e)}

# Test resolution for major domains
for host in ['google.com', 'cisco.com', 'uiu.ac.bd']:
    info = resolve_hostname(host)
    print(f"[*] Query: {host}")
    if 'error' in info:
        print(f"    Failed: {info['error']}")
    else:
        print(f"    Canonical: {info['canonical_name']}")
        print(f"    IPs      : {info['ip_addresses']}\n")

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Confusing CNAME with Type A: A Type A record maps a hostname directly to an IP Address (foo.com -> 1.2.3.4). A Type CNAME record maps an alias hostname to another Hostname (foo.com -> bar.com). * Assuming Root Servers return IP Addresses: Root servers almost NEVER return the final host IP! They return referrals (delegations) to TLD servers.

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 1, Page 29: Midterm 253 Q2)
docs.text:
Question: An application running on a host makes an iterative DNS query for www.university.net. Trace the queries and construct the resulting Local DNS Cache Table given: * Root DNS IP: 123.4.5.6 * .net TLD Name Server: admin.university.net, IP: 111.5.6.30 * Authoritative Name Server: ns1.university.net, IP: 203.0.113.2 * Target Host IP: www.university.net, IP: 203.0.113.10

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. Query Sequence: - Step 1: Client queries Local DNS server. - Step 2: Local DNS queries Root DNS (123.4.5.6). - Step 3: Root replies with referral to .net TLD (111.5.6.30). - Step 4: Local DNS queries .net TLD server (111.5.6.30). - Step 5: TLD replies with referral to Authoritative server ns1.university.net (203.0.113.2). - Step 6: Local DNS queries Authoritative server (203.0.113.2). - Step 7: Authoritative server replies with Type A record for www.university.net (203.0.113.10). - Step 8: Local DNS replies to Client with IP 203.0.113.10. 2. Local DNS Cache Table Construction: | Domain / Hostname | Cached Record Type & Value | |---|---| | . (Root) | 123.4.5.6 | | net | 111.5.6.30 (TLD Server) | | university.net | 203.0.113.2 (Authoritative NS) | | www.university.net | 203.0.113.10 (Type A Host IP) |

docs.title: Q1. Which DNS Resource Record type specifies the mail server responsible for receiving emails sent to a domain?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Type A
  • [ ] B) Type NS
  • [ ] C) Type CNAME
  • [x] D) Type MX Explanation: Type MX (Mail Exchange) records specify the mail server hostname for a given domain name.

docs.title: Q2. Why does DNS predominantly use UDP (Port 53) rather than TCP?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) UDP provides built-in encryption.
  • [x] B) DNS messages are small, and UDP avoids the connection setup latency (1 RTT) of TCP's 3-way handshake.
  • [ ] C) UDP guarantees in-order delivery.
  • [ ] D) Routers do not support TCP. Explanation: Lightweight UDP requests allow fast, low-latency queries without the overhead of maintaining connection state.

docs.title: Q3. A DNS query for www.example.com goes through the full iterative resolution chain. What is the correct query order?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Local DNS → Root → example.com TLD → Local Authoritative → Root again
  • [x] B) Local DNS → Root DNS Server → .com TLD Server → example.com Authoritative Server → Answer
  • [ ] C) Local DNS → example.com Authoritative directly
  • [ ] D) Root → TLD → Local DNS → Authoritative Explanation: Iterative DNS resolution: 1) Client asks Local DNS resolver. 2) Local DNS asks Root name server ("who handles .com?"). 3) Local DNS asks .com TLD server ("who handles example.com?"). 4) Local DNS asks example.com Authoritative server ("what is www.example.com?"). 5) Local DNS returns IP to client and caches the result with TTL.

docs.title: Q4. What is the difference between a DNS A record and a DNS CNAME record?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) A records are for IPv6, CNAME for IPv4 addresses
  • [x] B) An A record maps a hostname directly to an IPv4 address; a CNAME record maps a hostname to another hostname (canonical alias)
  • [ ] C) CNAME records are higher priority than A records
  • [ ] D) A records are authoritative; CNAME records are cached only Explanation: A record: www.example.com → 93.184.216.34 (hostname to IPv4). CNAME (Canonical Name): www.example.com → example.com (alias to canonical hostname). AAAA records are for IPv6. CNAME chains must eventually resolve to an A or AAAA record.

docs.title: Q5. Why does DNS primarily use UDP for queries rather than TCP?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) UDP provides guaranteed delivery which is required for DNS
  • [ ] B) TCP is too slow for internet communication
  • [x] C) DNS responses typically fit within a single UDP datagram (512 bytes for classic DNS, 4096+ with EDNS0); UDP avoids TCP's 3-way handshake overhead, making lookups faster
  • [ ] D) TCP cannot support the high query volume DNS servers handle Explanation: Most DNS responses fit in a single UDP datagram, so the reliability benefit of TCP's connection setup overhead (1 RTT for handshake) is not worth it. DNS handles its own reliability at the application layer — if no response arrives, the resolver retries the UDP query (typically 2-3 times before timing out). TCP is used for large zone transfers (AXFR) and responses exceeding 512 bytes.

docs.title: Q6. What is a DNS Amplification Attack and which DNS record type is most commonly exploited?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) An attack that floods DNS servers with recursive queries to exhaust their CPU
  • [x] B) A reflective DDoS attack where the attacker sends small DNS queries (with spoofed victim IP) to open resolvers; the resolvers send large responses (often ANY or TXT records) to the victim
  • [ ] C) An attack that injects false DNS records into the resolver cache
  • [ ] D) A botnet-based attack that purchases all available domain names Explanation: DNS Amplification exploits the size asymmetry: a 60-byte ANY query can generate a 3,000+ byte response — 50× amplification. The attacker spoofs the victim's IP, sends the small query to thousands of open recursive resolvers, which all send amplified responses to the victim. Mitigation: BCP38 source address validation, rate limiting DNS responses, disabling open recursion.

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• DNS Transport: UDP Port 53 (fast, connectionless).
  • Hierarchy: Root \(\to\) TLD (.com, .net, .edu, .bd) \(\to\) Authoritative \(\to\) Local DNS.
  • Iterative vs. Recursive: In Iterative, Local DNS visits servers step-by-step; in Recursive, contacted server resolves the entire query.
  • Resource Records:
  • Type A: (Hostname, IP)
  • Type NS: (Domain, NameServerHost)
  • Type CNAME: (AliasName, CanonicalName)
  • Type MX: (MailDomain, MailServerHost)

docs.title: ⚡ Module 04: Transport Layer and Reliability
docs.text: Welcome to Module 04: Transport Layer and Reliability. The Transport Layer bridges the gap between network-layer host-to-host packet delivery and application-layer process-to-process communication. This module covers Multiplexing/Demultiplexing, lightweight UDP and the 16-bit Internet Checksum, the theory of Reliable Data Transfer (RDT, Go-Back-N, Selective Repeat), the state-machine mechanics of TCP Connection Establishment & Termination, and the algorithms powering TCP Flow and Congestion Control (AIMD, Slow Start).

docs.title: 🔀 Chapter 01: Transport Layer Multiplexing and Demultiplexing
1. Overview (Topic Introduction)
docs.text: The Network Layer delivers datagrams between host computers (Host-to-Host delivery). However, on modern computers, dozens of distinct applications run concurrently (web browsers, game clients, email checkers, SSH sessions). The primary responsibility of the Transport Layer is to extend host-to-host delivery to Process-to-Process delivery between application processes running on those hosts. This is accomplished via Multiplexing (MUX) at the sender and Demultiplexing (DEMUX) at the receiver.

docs.title: 2. Learning Objectives
docs.text: After studying this chapter, you will be able to: * Distinguish between Host-to-Host delivery (Network Layer) and Process-to-Process delivery (Transport Layer). * Explain the mechanics of Multiplexing at the sender and Demultiplexing at the receiver. * Understand how Connectionless Demultiplexing (UDP) uses a 2-Tuple (Dest IP, Dest Port). * Understand how Connection-Oriented Demultiplexing (TCP) uses a 4-Tuple (Source IP, Source Port, Dest IP, Dest Port). * Trace concurrent client connections arriving at common service ports (e.g., HTTP Port 80/443, SMTP Port 587).

docs.title: 3.1 Multiplexing & Demultiplexing Defined
docs.text:
• Multiplexing at Sender (MUX): The task of gathering data chunks from different application sockets, encapsulating each chunk with transport headers (including source and destination port numbers), and passing the resulting segments to the Network Layer.
  • Demultiplexing at Receiver (DEMUX): The task of inspecting the header fields of an incoming transport segment delivered by the Network Layer and directing the payload to the correct receiving socket.
Sender Host (Multiplexing):                Receiver Host (Demultiplexing):
┌──────────────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ App 1   App 2   App 3 (Chrome)│          │ App 1   App 2   App 3 (Chrome)│
│   │       │       │          │          │   ▲       ▲       ▲          │
│   ▼       ▼       ▼          │          │   │       │       │          │
│ Socket1 Socket2 Socket3      │          │ Socket1 Socket2 Socket3      │
│   └───────┬───────┘          │          │   ▲       ▲       ▲          │
│           ▼                  │          │   └───────┼───────┘          │
│    [ MUX Engine ]            │          │    [ DEMUX Engine ]          │
│           │                  │          │           ▲                  │
│           ▼                  │          │           │                  │
│   Transport Layer (TCP/UDP)  │          │   Transport Layer (TCP/UDP)  │
│           │                  │          │           ▲                  │
│           ▼                  │          │           │                  │
│     Network Layer (IP)       │ ───────> │     Network Layer (IP)       │
└──────────────────────────────┘          └──────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 1. Connectionless Demultiplexing (UDP):
docs.text:
• A UDP socket is fully identified by a 2-Tuple: $\(\mathbf{(\text{Destination IP Address}, \ \text{Destination Port Number})}\)$
  • If two UDP segments arrive from different source IP addresses or different source port numbers, but have the same destination IP and destination port, they will both be directed to the exact same destination socket!

docs.title: 2. Connection-Oriented Demultiplexing (TCP):
docs.text:
• A TCP socket is uniquely identified by a 4-Tuple: $\(\mathbf{(\text{Source IP}, \ \text{Source Port}, \ \text{Destination IP}, \ \text{Destination Port})}\)$
  • When a TCP segment arrives from the network, the OS inspects all four values. Two incoming TCP segments with different source IP addresses or different source ports will be directed to two completely different welcoming sockets, even if both are targeting destination port 443!

docs.title: 5. Step-by-Step DEMUX Execution at Server
docs.text:
1. Physical & Data Link Arrival: Network interface card receives frames, removes MAC headers, passes IP datagrams to Network Layer.
  2. Network Layer Processing: Network layer checks destination IP address, verifies checksum, strips IP header, extracts the Transport Layer segment.
  3. Transport Layer Port Extraction: Transport layer parses the segment header to read:
  4. Source Port
  5. Destination Port
  6. Socket Table Lookup: The OS kernel searches its active socket table for an entry matching the 4-tuple (SrcIP, SrcPort, DstIP, DstPort).
  7. Buffer Delivery: The segment payload is placed directly into the matching socket’s receive buffer, waking up the waiting application process (recv() returns).

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Example
docs.text:
• University Mailroom Analogy:
  • The postal van delivers 500 letters to the University Administration Building (Network Layer Host Delivery).
  • The mailroom clerk reads the department and recipient name on each envelope (Transport Layer Header).
  • The clerk places Letter 1 into Professor Alice's pigeonhole (Port 443) and Letter 2 into Registrar Bob's pigeonhole (Port 587) (Demultiplexing).

docs.title: 7. Practical Implementation (Python 4-Tuple Socket Demux Verification)
docs.text:
import socket

def demonstrate_tcp_demux():
    # Server socket listening on port 8080
    server = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    server.bind(('127.0.0.1', 8080))
    server.listen(5)
    print("[*] Server welcoming socket listening on 127.0.0.1:8080")

    # The 4-tuple uniquely identifies each connection
    active_connections = {}

    def handle_connection(client_socket, client_address):
        # client_address is (client_ip, client_port)
        tuple_4 = (client_address[0], client_address[1], '127.0.0.1', 8080)
        active_connections[tuple_4] = client_socket
        print(f"[+] New dedicated socket spawned for 4-Tuple: {tuple_4}")

    print("[*] Ready to demultiplex incoming connections based on 4-tuples.")
    server.close()

demonstrate_tcp_demux()

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text: [!WARNING] * Assuming UDP uses 4-tuples for demuxing: UDP demuxing ignores source IP and source port when choosing the destination socket! All UDP packets targeting the same (DstIP, DstPort) land in the same socket. * Believing a Web Server on Port 80 can only talk to one client at a time: A web server listens on port 80. When a client connects, the OS creates a new dedicated socket identified by that unique 4-tuple, freeing the listening socket to welcome other clients concurrently!

docs.title: 📝 Problem 1 (From CN Class Note 2, Page 2: Midterm 261 Q1(b))
docs.text:
Question: Host A has IP 172.16.10.11 and Host B has IP 192.168.11.110. * Host A runs a browser connected from port 7000 to Google Web Server (142.251.211.78, port 443). * Host B runs a browser connected from port 8000 to Google Web Server (port 443). * Host B simultaneously runs an email client connected from port 9000 to Gmail Email Server (142.251.16.109, port 587). 1. Detail the 4-tuples for each of the three active TCP connections. 2. How does Google Web Server distinguish packets arriving from Host A versus Host B on port 443?

Step-by-Step Solution: 1. The Three 4-Tuples: * Connection 1 (Host A Browser \(\to\) Google Web Server): (172.16.10.11, 7000, 142.251.211.78, 443) * Connection 2 (Host B Browser \(\to\) Google Web Server): (192.168.11.110, 8000, 142.251.211.78, 443) * Connection 3 (Host B Email \(\to\) Gmail Email Server): (192.168.11.110, 9000, 142.251.16.109, 587) 2. Differentiation at Google Web Server: * Both Connection 1 and Connection 2 arrive with destination IP 142.251.211.78 and destination port 443. * However, the server's TCP demultiplexing engine examines the Source IP and Source Port: - Segments with (SrcIP: 172.16.10.11, SrcPort: 7000) are demultiplexed to Socket A. - Segments with (SrcIP: 192.168.11.110, SrcPort: 8000) are demultiplexed to Socket B.

docs.title: Q1. Which fields compose the 4-tuple used by an operating system to demultiplex incoming TCP segments?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) Source MAC, Destination MAC, Source IP, Destination IP
  • [ ] B) Source IP, Destination IP, Protocol, Checksum
  • [x] C) Source IP, Source Port, Destination IP, Destination Port
  • [ ] D) Sequence Number, Acknowledgement Number, Window, Flags Explanation: TCP connections are uniquely identified across the entire Internet by the 4-tuple of Source and Destination IP addresses and Port numbers.

docs.title: Q2. If two UDP datagrams have different Source IP addresses but the same Destination IP and Destination Port, what happens at the receiver?
docs.text:
• [ ] A) The second datagram is rejected as a collision.
  • [ ] B) A new socket is spawned for the second sender.
  • [x] C) Both datagrams are delivered to the exact same receiving socket.
  • [ ] D) The receiver converts the connection to TCP. Explanation: UDP demultiplexing is connectionless and based solely on the 2-tuple (Dest IP, Dest Port).

docs.title: 11. Summary & Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Multiplexing (Sender): Gathers data from multiple sockets, adds transport headers, passes to network layer.
  • Demultiplexing (Receiver): Inspects header ports, delivers segment data to correct socket.
  • UDP Demux: 2-Tuple (Dest IP, Dest Port).
  • TCP Demux: 4-Tuple (Src IP, Src Port, Dest IP, Dest Port).
